Recording work and active files use recording.bcast or recording.becast in per-recording directories, with a signed head.cbor. Published files are sealed/<base58-uuid-v4>.bcast or .becast. Remote targets copy those files byte for byte under <producer-id>/<sealed-file-name>.

The producer ID is SHA256(ssh-key), where ssh-key is the canonical binary SSH Ed25519 public-key blob. It is 32 raw bytes in the maps and 64 lowercase hex characters in paths. Recording IDs are 16 UUIDv4 bytes in CBOR; filenames use Base58 of those bytes. Producer IDs, hashes and fingerprints are not UUIDs.

A suffix, embedded signing key, or embedded producer ID is not an external trust anchor. Encryption does not replace Ed25519 signatures.

docs.title: Recording wire maps
docs.text:
Framing, event groups and checkpoints use version 1. The signed recording header selects UUID rendering for canonical Cast metadata and signature messages: version 2 uses Base58; version 1 uses canonical UUID notation. Each key below is an unsigned-integer CBOR map key. R means required, even for zero or false. O means omit when absent, never CBOR null. Types, canonical encoding, and head.cbor (a separately signed canonical map, not a container frame) follow the shared container rules.

timestamp is [i64 Unix seconds, u32 nanoseconds], with nanoseconds in 0..999999999. uuid16, hash32, and sig64 are byte strings of 16, 32, and 64 bytes. recipient is SHA256: plus unpadded standard Base64 of the 32-byte SSH recipient fingerprint.

docs.title: Header and chunk
docs.text:
Header (type 1) key Field Type Presence 1 header/UUID-rendering version u8 R 2 encryption (0 none, 1 age SSH) u8 R 3 recording ID uuid16 R 4 producer ID hash32 R 5 signing public key ssh-key R 6 start time timestamp R 7 recipient fingerprint (only for mode 1) recipient O 8 signature sig64 R Chunk (type 2) key Field Type Presence 1 sequence (starts at 1) u64 R 2 previous unit hash (header or preceding chunk frame) hash32 R 3 decoded CBOR event-group length u32 (positive) R 4 stored event group (Zstd frame or age message) nonempty bytes R 5 stored-byte hash hash32 R 6 Cast SHA-256 chaining state or final digest hash32 R 7 Cast SHA-256 processed byte count (0 for final) u64 R 8 signature sig64 R 9 final status (1 completed, 2 failed, 3 incomplete) u8 final only 10 final Cast digest (equals key 6) hash32 final only 11 standalone Cast signature sig64 final only 12 complete Cast export byte count (positive) u64 final only 13 end time timestamp final only 14 last actual event elapsed nanoseconds u64 continuation only

On a final chunk, keys 9..13 are all present and key 14 is absent. On a continuation, keys 9..13 are all absent and key 14 is present even when zero.

A continuation has nonzero, strictly increasing key 7 divisible by 64. A final chunk has key 7 = 0, and the hash in key 6 equals the Cast digest in key 10. The signed final chunk binds status, digest, Cast signature, complete Cast byte count and end time before a seal exists.

docs.title: Decoded event group
docs.text:
The decoded chunk is exactly {1: 1, 2: [event maps...]}. Key 1 is the event-group version; key 2 is a nonempty array of at most 4096 events. Each event has required key 1 (u8 kind) and only the fields below.

elapsed is an absolute, nonnegative nanosecond count (at most 10 * 365 * 24 hours), not a relative Cast line interval. A setup occurs exactly once first; a result occurs exactly once last. Nonfinal groups end in a padding event.

Event kind Required keys beyond 1 Optional keys Meaning 1 setup 2 Cast header map, 3 Cast metadata map none Initial Cast identity and terminal 2 output 2 elapsed u64, 3 stream u8 (1 terminal, 2 stdout, 3 stderr), 4 raw bytes (1..65536) none One output event 3 resize 2 elapsed u64, 3 columns u32, 4 rows u32 none Positive dimensions, at most 65535, PTY only 4 marker 2 elapsed u64, 3 label text none UTF-8 label, at most 4096 bytes 5 padding checkpoint none none Regenerates the Cast SHA-256 alignment comment 6 result 2 elapsed u64, 3 result map 4 exit status u32 Last event; exit status may be 0, at most 2147483647 Setup Cast header key Field Type Presence 1 Asciicast version (3) u8 R 2 terminal columns (1..65535) u32 R 3 terminal rows (1..65535) u32 R 4 terminal type (1..255 UTF-8 bytes) text O 5 Unix timestamp seconds (positive, equals metadata start seconds) u64 R Setup Cast metadata key Field Type Presence 1 recording ID (equals recording header) uuid16 R 2 connection ID 16-byte UUID bytes R 3 session ID 16-byte UUID bytes R 4 operation ID uuid16 R 5 flow text R 6 task (shell or exec) text R 7 PTY (including false) boolean R 8 producer ID (equals recording header) hash32 R 9 start time (equals recording header) timestamp R Result map key Field Type Presence 1 status (1 completed, 2 failed, 3 incomplete) u8 R 2 end time timestamp R 3 reason (1..255 UTF-8 bytes) text O

A completed result requires an exit status. Its end time must agree with the start plus elapsed time. All CastWriter stream, event-order, time and text validations apply across group boundaries.

Native groups contain no JSON or Asciicast lines; Cast rendering produces those only at export.

docs.title: Seal and recovery head
docs.text:
Seal (type 3) key Field Type Presence 1 final status u8 (1..3) R 2 chunk count (positive) u64 R 3 last chunk unit hash hash32 R 4 content hash hash32 R 5 Cast digest hash32 R 6 standalone Cast signature sig64 R 7 complete Cast export bytes (positive) u64 R 8 end time timestamp R 9 signature sig64 R Recording head key Field Type Presence 1 version (1) u8 R 2 recording ID uuid16 R 3 producer ID hash32 R 4 durable prefix length (magic + header + committed continuation chunks) u64 R 5 continuation chunk count (positive) u64 R 6 last unit hash hash32 R 7 Cast SHA-256 chaining state hash32 R 8 Cast SHA-256 processed bytes (positive, divisible by 64) u64 R 9 signature sig64 R

The seal must exactly match the final chunk. The head records an exact durable continuation prefix, not a final chunk or an alternative source of events.

docs.title: Recording identity and chain
docs.text: The recording header binds version, mode, recording ID, producer ID, public key, start time, and any recipient fingerprint. Signed outer chunk descriptors bind sequence, previous unit hash, stored payload hash, decoded byte count, and the continuation information required by encrypted offline recovery. The seal binds status, counts, the last unit hash, the content hash, and the pre-established signature of the exact canonical .cast export.

docs.title: Sign each map
docs.text:
Recording header, chunk, seal and head signatures each equal Ed25519.sign(D_signature || C(map without signature key)) (key 8, 8, 9 and 9 respectively). C is exact canonical CBOR; || denotes byte concatenation. Optional keys are included only if present.

These literal ASCII domains include the terminal NUL (\x00) and are distinct from the audit domains:

BIFROEST-BCAST-HEADER-SIGNATURE/v1\x00
BIFROEST-BCAST-CHUNK-SIGNATURE/v1\x00
BIFROEST-BCAST-SEAL-SIGNATURE/v1\x00
BIFROEST-BCAST-HEAD-SIGNATURE/v1\x00
BIFROEST-BCAST-UNIT-HASH/v1\x00
BIFROEST-BCAST-CONTENT-HASH/v1\x00

docs.title: Hash committed frames
docs.text:
For recording magic R (seven bytes), with F the exact complete committed state-1 frame (including CRC and marker), calculate:

stored_hash       = SHA256(chunk[4])              # plain SHA-256, NO domain
header_unit_hash  = SHA256(D_recording_unit_hash || F(header))
chunk_i_unit_hash = SHA256(D_recording_unit_hash || F(chunk_i))
content_hash      = SHA256(D_recording_content_hash || R || F(header) || F(chunk_1) || ... || F(chunk_n))

Chunk 1 key 2 equals header_unit_hash; each later key 2 equals the prior chunk_i_unit_hash. The seal key 3 equals the last chunk unit hash. Its key 4 hashes from offset zero through the byte immediately before the seal: magic, header and all committed chunks, but not the seal.

Neither chain hash includes the magic; the content hash does. There is no recording equivalent of the audit sealed-segment hash. The recording head key 4 is the exact physical prefix length at the end of a committed continuation frame. Keys 5..8 must match that prefix's chunk count, last unit hash and last Cast checkpoint.

docs.title: Cast checkpoint and signature
docs.text:
For a nonfinal chunk, Cast key 6 is the 32 raw SHA-256 internal chaining-state bytes at a 64-byte block boundary, not a digest. These are the eight state words H0 through H7 in that order, each encoded as a big-endian 32-bit integer, before SHA-256 final padding.

Key 7 is the total number of bytes fed to SHA-256. It includes the literal BIFROEST-ASCIICAST-CONTENT-HASH/v1\x00 prefix and all rendered Cast content through that chunk's padding line and LF. It is positive, increasing and divisible by 64.

The padding line has prefix # becast-checkpoint-padding:v1, followed by the unique 0..63 ASCII zeros needed so (processed_bytes + len(padding_prefix) + zeros + 1 LF) % 64 == 0. No SHA-256 partial block is retained in the signed checkpoint.

On a final chunk key 7 is zero and key 6 is the completed Cast digest (key 10), not a resumable state. Key 12 and seal key 7 count complete .cast bytes including the final signature comment and its LF; unlike Cast key 7 they exclude the hash domain. The Cast digest instead covers the domain plus exact Cast lines through the result line and LF, excluding the signature comment.

The standalone Cast uses schema bifroest.asciicast-signature/v1 and domains BIFROEST-ASCIICAST-CONTENT-HASH/v1\x00 and BIFROEST-ASCIICAST-SIGNATURE/v1\x00. Its Ed25519 signature covers the signature domain plus canonical JSON signature content (schema, recordingId, producerId, lowercase hex digest, and binary SSH publicKey as Base64).

The native seal stores that signature and digest. No JSON or Cast line is stored inside the native recording. Offline export must reproduce and verify the same bytes without the server's signing key. See Canonical standalone Cast for rendering rules.

docs.title: Encode and bound each group
docs.text:
Each recording event-group is canonical CBOR, encoded as canonical CBOR -> one Zstd frame -> (mode 1 only) one independent age SSH message -> stored CBOR byte string. The header binds mode and recipient; chunk signatures bind stored bytes. There is no raw-CBOR fallback.

Each Zstd frame has a checksum, declared decoded size, no dictionary, a maximum 2 MiB window and at most 32 blocks. Reject skippable/concatenated frames and trailing bytes. Authenticate each age message through EOF before accepting the decoded group. Header and seal are uncompressed CBOR units.

  • A decoded group is at most 2 MiB. The complete stored chunk CBOR payload is at most 4 MiB excluding its 18 framing bytes. The stored byte string is at most 4 MiB - 256 bytes. The default decoded-group target is 256 KiB.
  • Recording container, Cast, and chunk-count defaults are 32 GiB, 16 GiB, and 262144 chunks. Configured lower limits still apply. Readers enforce encoded and decoded limits before publishing data.

docs.title: Resume from the signed prefix
docs.text:
The signed head.cbor keys 4..8 must match the exact committed continuation prefix. Verify each committed successor before advancing recovery. A committed final chunk supplies its signed status, digest, signature and end time when writing a missing seal.

Otherwise recovery resumes the last signed, block-aligned Cast SHA-256 state, appending a clear or encrypted incomplete-result chunk with no exit event. It uses the last signed event elapsed time, without inventing output or timing.

A continuation without a persisted head fails closed. With no head, seal only an otherwise complete, verified chain ending in a committed final chunk with no uncommitted tail.

Only uncommitted tails after the checkpoint may be truncated. A physically complete state-0 unit needs valid framing, CRC and canonical CBOR and no bytes after its declared boundary. For a physically short state-0 tail, a bounded overlap search must rule out any plausible committed state-1 unit even with damaged CRC.

An invalid committed unit, overlapping candidate, state-0 tail before the checkpoint, or extra bytes fails closed.

docs.title: Persist committed units
docs.text:
Recovery requires an exclusively locked, writable WriteAt file. Its core performs body-Sync and commit-byte-Sync; the caller syncs the directory after publication.

NativeDurableRecordingOutput accepts an empty regular read/write file without O_APPEND. It syncs magic, then writes each signed unit with state 0, syncs, sets state 1 with WriteAt and syncs again. Physical byte counts and content hashes use state-1 frames.

A failed append poisons the sink until recovery. Passing a bare *os.File to the writer is rejected, and the in-memory io.Writer path is not durable. The repository adapter supplies locking, quota, signed-head replacement and directory sync. Neither a local head nor an artifact stored beside it prevents rollback of both without an external anchor.

docs.title: Choose the verification level
docs.text:
Outer verification checks signed frames, CRC, identities, hashes, stored-byte commitments and seal without age keys. For clear payloads it also decompresses and checks canonical CBOR; recovery checks clear event maps.

For encrypted payloads, outer verification cannot attest decrypted events or Cast semantics: status and Cast digest are signed outer claims. Full verification decrypts/authenticates when needed, validates all events, renders the exact Cast, verifies its digest and standalone signature, and checks every Cast checkpoint.

Both modes require an independently trusted expected producer ID; a content-supplied key is not that trust anchor.

docs.title: Verify before export
docs.text:
Offline FullVerify/Export requires the same immutable io.ReaderAt snapshot across passes. It verifies the outer container, then streams independently authenticated/decompressed groups (at most 2 MiB decoded each) through the renderer to the Cast verifier. It checks signed continuations, final digest/signature, result and exact byte count before exporting bytes.

Export rereads the same snapshot in a second bounded pass, without buffering the full Cast or writing sensitive temporary plaintext. A mid-write destination failure can leave a partial verified Cast; atomic publication belongs to the caller.

RenderNativeRecordingCast returning []byte is an in-memory helper, not the large-artifact export path. Never automatically generate a .cast or .jsonl on disk or at remote targets; operator export requires explicit --with-sensitive.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Choose the task you want to accomplish:

  • SSH gateway to an OpenSSH server: authenticate at Bifröst, then connect to a private SSH target.
  • SSH over HTTPS with OpenSSH and curl: connect through HTTPS or WSS without a separate tunnel client.
  • OIDC login: sign in through your IdP and open a container session via SSH or the WebUI.
  • Test a configuration: write Lua expectations for offline flow selection and target mapping, then export CI reports.
  • Browser access: enable HTTPS and open a browser shell as an existing local account.
  • Manage a Bifröst host remotely: configure workload and administration flows, then inspect live state from a workstation.
  • Export server public keys remotely: retrieve configured public SSH identities, certificate authorities and active host keys through management access.
  • Record, find and replay a session: capture terminal output, find the sealed original and verify, play or export it.
  • Verify encrypted evidence on a workstation: configure encrypted audit and Recording data, pin producer trust and keep decryption local.
  • Monitor a Bifröst instance: scrape Prometheus metrics and configure Kubernetes startup, readiness and liveness probes.

Install Bifröst first using the host installation guide, and use the guide from the same release as your binary. Each example requires you to provide your own identities and permissions; none replaces the configuration reference.

Not sure which setup fits? See Choosing Bifröst and Security and trust.

docs.title: Browser access
docs.text:
Open a shell on a Bifröst host with a browser instead of an SSH client. HTTPS access is optional and can run alongside SSH.

This Linux example requires the extended release installed as a host service, running as root, and an existing local account alice whose password is accepted by /etc/pam.d/sshd.

Point bifroest.example.org at the host and make TCP port 443 publicly reachable. Bifröst obtains and renews its certificate through ACME; TLS must terminate directly at Bifröst.

docs.title: Configure HTTPS and a terminal flow
docs.text:
Use the following configuration with your hostname, contact email and local account. Review the certificate authority's terms before setting acceptTerms: true. Keep another way to access the host while changing its service.

Bifröst host: /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
http:
  enabled: true
  addresses: [":443"]
  domains: [bifroest.example.org]
  tls:
    acme:
      enabled: true
      acceptTerms: true
      email: operator@example.org

flows:
  - name: local
    discoverAsSlug: Shell
    http:
      requestUser: true
    requirement:
      includedRequestingName: ^alice$
      http:
        includedSlug: '^Shell$'
    authorization:
      type: local
      rememberMe: allowedAndEnabledByDefault
      password:
        allowed: true
        emptyAllowed: false
    environment:
      type: local
      name: "{{.authorization.user.name}}"
      portForwardingAllowed: false

The flow authenticates alice and opens the shell as that verified local account. No account is created and no password belongs in the configuration.

Review every flow before enabling HTTPS

Enabling HTTP makes all flows HTTP-eligible by default. On an existing deployment, merge these settings and set http: {enabled: false} on each flow that must remain SSH-only.

Restart the service:

sudo systemctl restart bifroest.service

docs.title: Open your first shell
docs.text:
1. Open https://bifroest.example.org/#Shell and check the address and certificate.
  2. Choose Password, enter alice and its password, then select Sign in. Leave Remember this browser unchecked for this first login.

  3. In the new terminal, check the account and finish the shell:

    id -un
exit

    id -un should print alice; a successful exit closes the terminal tab. If login fails, check the account's status and the host's PAM policy.

Reloading opens a new shell, not the old execution. Closing a tab is not logout; choose Log out to revoke browser access. The example enables RememberMe by default; clear Remember this browser before login to opt out.

In terminals, use Ctrl+Shift+C to copy selected text and Ctrl+Shift+V to paste. Ctrl+C remains interrupt/cancel. Clipboard access may require browser permission.

docs.title: Access links and hidden Slugs
docs.text:
Use https://bifroest.example.org/#alice@Shell to prefill the user name. Editing the user name updates the link without reloading; email-style names are encoded, for example #alice%40example.org@Shell. User names in shared links are visible to their recipients and may be retained in browser history and bookmarks. They are hints, not verified identities.

Prefilled user names are also reflected in the link when a name-based login method is selected. After login, each tab and its copied access link retain that access's original requesting name, including after saved-login resumption. This name is separate from the identity verified by an external IdP. A missing required name is marked directly at its field.

The Slug field accepts free input as well as published suggestions. Enter a Slug and press Enter, or choose a suggestion. An unknown Slug is marked as invalid directly at the field; network and server errors remain separate and can be retried.

For a hidden link, omit discoverAsSlug and explicitly allow its Slug through requirement.http.includedSlug. A password manager can generate a long random alphanumeric Slug. Hidden Slugs are not listed to other visitors, but still require the flow's normal authentication and authorization.

Slugs and optional user names stay in the browser fragment, not document paths or request query strings. Discovery sends the Slug in a JSON body to POST /api/v1/discovery; other API calls also use request bodies, and WebSocket channels send it in their opening message. This keeps Slugs out of ordinary URL access logs, not out of explicitly configured body logging. Paths such as /Shell are not access links and return 404.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Manage a host remotely adds a management flow; terminal access alone grants no management access.
  • Record, find and replay a session enables optional output recording and verification.
  • HTTP configuration covers other deployment choices.

docs.title: Verify encrypted evidence on a workstation
docs.text:
This example creates encrypted audit events and Recordings on a Linux Bifröst host, then verifies and exports them on an administrator's workstation. The server receives the recipient's public key. The private decryption key and plaintext exports stay on the workstation.

The management login uses a separate SSH identity and trusted host key as in the remote-management guide. Use a new, empty evidence journal and Recording directory for this example. Existing histories cannot switch encryption recipient in place.

docs.title: Configure the recipient and server
docs.text:
1. On the trusted verification workstation, prepare private directories /srv/audit-keys and /srv/audit-evidence, owned by the intended verification operator. Have the workstation administrator provision them if necessary. Create a dedicated recipient key pair as that operator:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest key generate \
  --identityFile /srv/audit-keys/recipient-key \
  --publicFile /srv/audit-keys/recipient-key.pub

  2. Transfer only recipient-key.pub to the Bifröst host as /etc/engity/bifroest/evidence-recipient.pub. Provision the management login's public key in /etc/engity/bifroest/management_authorized_keys. Neither the recipient private key nor the management login private key belongs in this server configuration.

  3. Configure the evidence and administration flows:

    Bifröst host: /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
    auditlogs:
  evidence:
    identityFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/evidence-signing-key
    directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/evidence-audit
    encryptionPublicKeyFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/evidence-recipient.pub
    recording:
      enabled: true
      directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/evidence-recordings

  administration:
    identityFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/administration-signing-key
    directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/administration-audit
    recording:
      directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/administration-recordings

flows:
  - name: administration
    auditlog: administration
    requirement:
      includedRequestingName: ^management$
    authorization:
      type: simple
      entries:
        - name: management
          authorizedKeysFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/management_authorized_keys
    environment:
      type: management
      access:
        auditlogs:
          read: true
          events: true
          verify: true
          download: true
        recordings: true

  - name: local
    auditlog: evidence
    requirement:
      excludedRequestingName: ^management$
    authorization:
      type: local
    environment:
      type: local
      name: "{{.authorization.user.name}}"
      portForwardingAllowed: false

    This access object grants audit and Recording operations, including original signed evidence, but no session control or configuration credentials. The CLI still requires --with-sensitive before displaying or exporting private content.

  4. Restart Bifröst using the host's service manager. The new evidence journal stores .beaudit; sealed Recordings use .becast. The separate administration journal in this example remains unencrypted.

  5. As the Bifröst service user, obtain the evidence producer ID from its signing identity:

    Bifröst host
    bifroest audit producer-id evidence

    Transfer and retain this 64-hex value through an independently trusted channel. Keep the server's signing private key on the server; do not derive producer trust from downloaded evidence.

docs.title: Configure the verification workstation
docs.text:
1. Provision the trusted SSH host key and management login identity as in the management guide.

  2. Add the producer pin and local decryption paths. Replace PRODUCER_ID with the independently retained ID:

    Verification workstation: ~/.ssh/config
    IgnoreUnknown X-*

Host bifroest-admin
    HostName bifroest.example.org
    User management
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bifroest-management
    UserKnownHostsFile ~/.ssh/known_hosts
    X-ExpectedProducerId PRODUCER_ID
    X-AuditPrivateKey /srv/audit-keys/recipient-key
    X-RecordingPrivateKey /srv/audit-keys/recipient-key

    The SSH login key and recipient key have separate purposes. Both private-key paths refer to the workstation. This alias pins the producer of evidence; other audit logs with different signing identities need their own trusted ID or alias.

  3. Generate an actual Recording through the workload flow:

    Workload terminal
    ssh alice@bifroest.example.org 'printf "encrypted-recording-check\n"'

    Replace alice with an allowed local account.

docs.title: Verify and export audit events
docs.text:
1. On the workstation, verify the downloaded journal and decrypted event fields:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin audit verify evidence --require-full --format=json

    A successful result has full scope. The recipient private key is read locally and is not transmitted to the server.

  2. Query a limited sensitive view, or export the journal to a protected, existing output directory:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin audit events evidence --with-sensitive --flow=local --limit=20
bifroest @bifroest-admin audit export evidence \
  --with-sensitive \
  --output /srv/audit-evidence/events.jsonl

    The output JSONL is plaintext and unsigned. Preserve the original signed journal as evidence; an export is a derived view.

docs.title: Verify, export and replay a Recording
docs.text:
1. Find the sealed original:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin recording ls evidence --limit=20
bifroest @bifroest-admin recording show evidence RECORDING_UUID

    Replace RECORDING_UUID with the selected ID. These metadata queries receive outer verification of encrypted Recordings and do not need to decrypt them.

  2. Download and fully verify that Recording:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin recording verify evidence RECORDING_UUID --require-full

    The client checks the trusted producer and the requested Recording ID against the signed original.

  3. Export its verified Cast, then inspect the export independently:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin recording export evidence RECORDING_UUID \
  --with-sensitive \
  --output /srv/audit-evidence/session.cast
bifroest recording inspect \
  --expectedProducerId PRODUCER_ID \
  /srv/audit-evidence/session.cast

  4. Or replay the selected original directly on the workstation:

    Verification workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin recording play evidence RECORDING_UUID --with-sensitive --speed=2

    play outputs terminal content; export writes a signed asciicast file. Both fully verify the encrypted content before playback or export.

docs.title: Browser alternative
docs.text:
Enable HTTPS as in Browser access, then publish the administration flow with discoverAsSlug: Admin and requirement.http.includedSlug: '^Admin$'. Keep its requesting-name requirement and the access object above.

  1. Open https://bifroest.example.org/#Admin and sign in through SSH key as management.
  2. Choose Audit logs, select evidence, then open Events or Recordings.
  3. Start local verification, select the recipient key and enter its passphrase. Enable signing-ID validation with your independently retained producer ID, not merely the suggested server value.

The decryption key stays in this management tab and is discarded when it closes. Browser code is served by the server; use the CLI workflow above when the verification tool must be independently trusted.

docs.title: Offline alternatives
docs.text: If the verification workstation is disconnected from the server, copy a complete audit journal or a sealed Recording and use local file selectors with the same independent producer ID and recipient key. Follow the encrypted audit-copy example or the file syntax on recording verify.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Trust and verification covers key-file permissions, evidence completeness, verification scopes and protected destinations.
  • Remote targets reference explains off-host delivery of sealed originals.
  • The audit and recording command references describe all inspection, verification and export options.

docs.title: Export server public keys remotely
docs.text:
This Linux example configures a certificate-authenticated SSH gateway and a separate management flow. An administrator exports the gateway's existing public identities to a workstation. Private keys stay on their source machines. Management access also permits session disconnection and disposal; it is not read-only.

Start with an installed Bifröst host, separate login keys for the administrator and alice, and an OpenSSH target for alice at target.example.org. Obtain the target host keys through a trusted provisioning channel. The first management connection also needs an independently trusted Bifröst host-key entry; remote key export cannot establish its own initial host trust.

docs.title: Configure the management and gateway flows
docs.text:
1. Provision these public files on the Bifröst host:

    File Initial content /etc/engity/bifroest/management_authorized_keys Administrator's public login key. /etc/engity/bifroest/gateway-clients.pub Alice's public login key for Bifröst. /etc/engity/bifroest/target_known_hosts Independently trusted host-key entries for target.example.org.

    Make the files readable by the service user. Keep the administrator's private login key on the workstation as ~/.ssh/bifroest-management. The target's CA configuration follows after exporting the gateway CA below.

  2. Configure the Bifröst host:

    Bifröst host: /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
    flows:
  - name: administration
    requirement:
      includedRequestingName: ^management$
    authorization:
      type: simple
      entries:
        - name: management
          authorizedKeysFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/management_authorized_keys
    environment:
      type: management

  - name: gateway
    requirement:
      includedRequestingName: ^alice$
    authorization:
      type: simple
      entries:
        - name: alice
          authorizedKeysFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/gateway-clients.pub
    environment:
      type: ssh
      address: target.example.org
      user: alice
      knownHostsFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/target_known_hosts
      certificate:
        identityFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/gateway-subject
        authorityIdentityFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/gateway-ca

    management selects the administration flow, and alice selects the gateway. The default management access object grants keys.read for public key exports. Alice's incoming login key, the gateway's outbound certificate CA, and target host trust have separate roles.

  3. Start or restart Bifröst through the host's service manager. Startup loads the provisioned trust and ensures the configured gateway subject and CA identities. Remote exports will only use these existing keys.

  4. After provisioning Bifröst's host key in the workstation's ~/.ssh/known_hosts, add the login alias:

    Administrator workstation: ~/.ssh/config
    Host bifroest-admin
    HostName bifroest.example.org
    User management
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bifroest-management
    UserKnownHostsFile ~/.ssh/known_hosts

docs.title: Export the running server's public keys
docs.text:
1. Export the gateway's CA and subject public identity:

    Administrator workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin key export ca gateway --output gateway-ca.pub
bifroest @bifroest-admin key export public gateway --output gateway-subject.pub

    These output files are on the workstation. Provision the exported CA at the OpenSSH target to trust the gateway's outbound certificates for alice, following the certificate-authentication example. A remote export never creates or replaces a missing server key.

  2. Export Bifröst's active host keys, labeling them with its externally used address:

    Administrator workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin key export host \
  --address bifroest.example.org \
  --output bifroest-known-hosts

    Use --force only when replacing an existing workstation output file is intended. Server trust files are maintained through normal configuration management.

docs.title: Use a standard SSH client
docs.text:
1. Use the same management authorization and trusted host key with a standard SSH client:

    Administrator workstation
    ssh management@bifroest.example.org 'key export ca gateway' > gateway-ca.pub
ssh management@bifroest.example.org 'key export public gateway' > gateway-subject.pub
ssh management@bifroest.example.org 'key export host --address=bifroest.example.org' > bifroest-known-hosts

    Supply the login identity or agent required by that SSH client. Direct SSH writes public exports to stdout; choose the workstation destination through the SSH client's output redirection.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Key reference documents per-command arguments and invocation modes.
  • Management permissions describes the separate access controls.
  • Bifröst delegation configures certificate trust between Bifröst instances.

docs.title: Manage a Bifröst host remotely
docs.text:
This Linux example adds a dedicated management flow alongside a local-account workload flow. Workload and administration events go to different audit logs. The management connection can inspect metadata without downloading signed evidence.

Start with an installed Bifröst host, a local account allowed to use the workload flow, and a separate SSH key for administrator login. The paths below assume the host configuration uses /etc/engity/bifroest and /var/lib/engity/bifroest. Other platforms have different defaults.

docs.title: Configure remote administration
docs.text:
1. Provision the administrator's public login key in /etc/engity/bifroest/management_authorized_keys. Keep the corresponding private key on the workstation as ~/.ssh/bifroest-management. Make the server file readable by the Bifröst service user and writable only by the administrator responsible for configuration.

  2. Configure two audit logs and two flows:

    Bifröst host: /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
    auditlogs:
  workload:
    identityFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/workload-signing-key
    directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/workload-audit
    recording:
      enabled: true
      directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/workload-recordings

  administration:
    identityFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/administration-signing-key
    directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/administration-audit
    recording:
      directory: /var/lib/engity/bifroest/administration-recordings

flows:
  - name: administration
    auditlog: administration
    requirement:
      includedRequestingName: ^management$
    authorization:
      type: simple
      rememberMe: allowedAndEnabledByDefault
      entries:
        - name: management
          authorizedKeysFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/management_authorized_keys
    environment:
      type: management

  - name: local
    auditlog: workload
    requirement:
      excludedRequestingName: ^management$
    authorization:
      type: local
      rememberMe: allowedAndEnabledByDefault
    environment:
      type: local
      name: "{{.authorization.user.name}}"
      portForwardingAllowed: false

    management selects only the administration flow. Other requesting names can use local-account authorization. Journal and Recording paths are separate, and each auditlog has its own signing identity. The default strict failure policy applies.

  3. Restart Bifröst using the host's service manager. On first start with empty repositories, Bifröst creates the configured signing keys and storage. Retain existing identity and repository files on subsequent starts.

  4. Obtain the host's SSH public key through a trusted provisioning channel and install its matching known_hosts entry on the workstation. Add a login alias:

    Administrator workstation: ~/.ssh/config
    Host bifroest-admin
    HostName bifroest.example.org
    User management
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/bifroest-management
    UserKnownHostsFile ~/.ssh/known_hosts

    Replace the hostname with the actual host. The integrated client requires an already trusted host key; it does not accept an unknown key automatically.

  5. Inspect the server from the workstation:

    Administrator workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin flow ls
bifroest @bifroest-admin flow show administration --format=yaml
bifroest @bifroest-admin audit ls
bifroest @bifroest-admin audit events administration --limit=20

    Settings are redacted and original downloads are disabled. The default management permissions also allow session control; use an explicit access object to restrict operations.

docs.title: Find a workload session and its Recording
docs.text:
1. Using a standard SSH client and an allowed host account, open a workload shell:

    Workload terminal
    ssh alice@bifroest.example.org

    Replace alice with the actual requesting username. Leave this shell open for the next step.

  2. Inspect that session from the administration workstation:

    Administrator workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin session ls --flow=local --user=alice --format=json
bifroest @bifroest-admin session show SESSION_UUID

    Replace SESSION_UUID with an ID from the listing. The flow filter excludes the administration session itself.

  3. In the workload shell, print a marker and exit:

    Workload terminal
    printf 'recording-check\n'
exit

  4. Find the sealed Recording and inspect its metadata:

    Administrator workstation
    bifroest @bifroest-admin recording ls workload --limit=20
bifroest @bifroest-admin recording show workload RECORDING_UUID --format=json

    Use the returned Recording UUID, which is distinct from the session UUID. Listing order is by Recording ID, not start time; use the reported timestamps when choosing a Recording.

  5. The same metadata query is available through a standard SSH client:

    Administrator workstation
    ssh management@bifroest.example.org 'recording ls workload --limit=20'

    Supply the appropriate OpenSSH identity or agent for this separate connection. Direct SSH executes a management command and does not open a host shell.

docs.title: Disconnect or dispose of a workload session
docs.text:
Find the workload session with session ls, then choose one action:

  • Close its current SSH and browser connections but keep the session reusable:

    bifroest @bifroest-admin session disconnect SESSION_UUID

  • Revoke it, disconnect it and run its configured cleanup:

    bifroest @bifroest-admin session dispose SESSION_UUID

Disposal can remove containers, Pods or managed accounts and home directories, depending on the environment. This example grants sessions.disconnect and sessions.dispose through the default access object. A command cannot target its own executing management session. See disconnect and dispose for details and failure behavior.

docs.title: Browser alternative
docs.text:
Enable HTTPS as in Browser access. Publish the administration flow with discoverAsSlug: Admin and requirement.http.includedSlug: '^Admin$', keeping its existing requesting-name requirement.

  1. Open https://bifroest.example.org/#Admin, choose SSH key and sign in as management with the workstation's login key.
  2. Choose Sessions, filter for the workload flow and open the desired session.
  3. Choose Disconnect connections or End session and confirm the exact target. These perform the same operations as the CLI commands above.

This example permits public browser event queries and Recording metadata, but not original downloads or playback. For controlled downloads and local decryption, follow encrypted evidence.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Verify encrypted evidence on a workstation enables controlled artifact transfer and keeps decryption local.
  • Remote-access reference documents SSH agents, custom settings and permissions.
  • Management environment properties describe the server-side access controls.

docs.title: Monitor a Bifröst instance
docs.text: This guide queries metrics from an installed, configured Bifröst instance through management SSH or an existing Prometheus installation. Prometheus scraping and Kubernetes probes do not require browser or management access. The monitoring reference defines all settings and metric semantics.

docs.title: Query metrics through management SSH
docs.text:
1. Set up the management flow and workstation alias. No monitoring listener or Prometheus installation is needed for this example.

  2. Query the running instance:

    bifroest @bifroest-admin metrics show bifroest_connections_active bifroest_sessions_active

    The default table shows current values and labels. For scripts or an OpenMetrics snapshot, use --format=json or --format=openmetrics. Omit metric names to show all available families. See metrics show for filtering and output details.

docs.title: Scrape a host locally
docs.text:
1. Add the monitoring block to the existing Bifröst configuration:

    Bifröst configuration
    monitoring:
  enabled: true
  addresses: ["localhost:9090"]

    Restart Bifröst using the host's service manager. If Prometheus also listens on this host, configure a different port for one of the listeners.

  2. Check readiness and metrics from the same host:

    Bifröst host
    curl --fail http://localhost:9090/ready
curl --fail http://localhost:9090/metrics

    /ready returns ready after startup. Metrics include bifroest_ready 1.

  3. Add a scrape job to the local Prometheus configuration and reload Prometheus:

    prometheus.yml
    scrape_configs:
  - job_name: bifroest
    scrape_interval: 15s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["localhost:9090"]

    In Prometheus, check up{job="bifroest"} and bifroest_ready. Both should be 1. Scrape each instance separately; do not hide individual instances behind a load-balanced scrape target.

docs.title: Use a bearer token
docs.text:
1. Mount or provision the same secret token in separate private files readable by Bifröst and Prometheus. Add its path to Bifröst:

    Bifröst configuration
    monitoring:
  enabled: true
  bearerTokenFile: /run/secrets/monitoring-token

  2. Configure Prometheus to send it:

    Prometheus scrape job
    job_name: bifroest
authorization:
  credentials_file: /run/secrets/bifroest-monitoring-token
static_configs:
  - targets: ["localhost:9090"]

    Restart Bifröst and reload Prometheus. /metrics now requires the token; the minimal /ready and /status probes remain token-free. For remote scraping, configure a private reachable address, an appropriate peer allowlist and TLS or an encrypted network. HTTP alone does not protect the token from interception.

docs.title: Configure Kubernetes probes
docs.text:
1. In the Bifröst Pod's existing configuration, bind monitoring to the Pod network:

    Bifröst configuration
    monitoring:
  enabled: true
  addresses: [":9090"]
  allowedRemoteHosts: []

    Restrict this port through your cluster networking policy and do not publish it externally. An empty allowlist permits every reachable peer. If you configure IP/CIDR entries, include the actual Prometheus and node/probe source ranges, not just the Pod network.

  2. Add the named port and probes to the existing Bifröst container specification:

    Bifröst container fragment
    ports:
  - name: monitoring
    containerPort: 9090
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: monitoring
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
  failureThreshold: 60
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: monitoring
  periodSeconds: 5
  timeoutSeconds: 2
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /status
    port: monitoring
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 2

    This allows roughly five minutes for startup before Kubernetes restarts the container. Adjust the budget to your deployment. Startup gates the other probes; readiness failures remove the Pod from normal Service traffic without themselves causing a restart. A slow IdP or failed remote delivery does not deliberately fail liveness. With monitoring TLS enabled, set scheme: HTTPS on each HTTP probe; Kubernetes HTTPS probes do not validate the server certificate.

  3. Roll out the updated Pod specification and inspect its readiness with kubectl get pods. Configure your existing Prometheus discovery to scrape each Pod's monitoring port at /metrics, including bearer authorization if enabled.

docs.title: Add operational alerts
docs.text:
Add these example rules to your existing Prometheus rule group and adapt the thresholds:

Prometheus alert rules
groups:
  - name: bifroest
    rules:
      - alert: BifroestMetricsUnavailable
        expr: up{job="bifroest"} == 0
        for: 2m
      - alert: BifroestAuditlogDisabled
        expr: bifroest_auditlog_disabled == 1
        for: 1m
      - alert: BifroestRecordingSpoolPressure
        expr: bifroest_recording_spool_bytes / bifroest_recording_spool_limit_bytes > 0.85
        for: 5m
      - alert: BifroestRecordingAccountingUnavailable
        expr: bifroest_recording_spool_accounting_valid == 0
        for: 2m
      - alert: BifroestDeliveryStalled
        expr: bifroest_remote_delivery_pending_observed_seconds > 300
        for: 2m
      - alert: BifroestCleanupFailing
        expr: bifroest_cleanup_problems > 0 or bifroest_cleanup_last_run_success{operation="housekeeping"} == 0
        for: 15m
      - alert: BifroestJournalSpaceLow
        expr: (bifroest_auditlog_available_bytes < bifroest_auditlog_minimum_free_bytes * 2) and on (job, instance, auditlog) (bifroest_auditlog_space_observation_valid == 1) and on (job, instance, auditlog) (time() - bifroest_auditlog_space_observation_timestamp_seconds < 60)
        for: 2m
      - alert: BifroestHttpCertificateExpiring
        expr: bifroest_http_tls_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds - time() < 7 * 86400
        for: 5m
      - alert: BifroestHttpServerErrors
        expr: sum by (job, instance) (rate(bifroest_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum by (job, instance) (rate(bifroest_http_requests_total[5m])) > 0.05
        for: 5m

An unavailable scrape can mean a network, authorization or listener problem; it is not proof that workload access has failed. Resolve a disabled best-effort logger's cause and restart Bifröst to re-enable it. The delivery alert detects observed worker stalls, not a complete historical delivery backlog.

For access/security dashboards, use sum by (transport, result) (rate(bifroest_authentication_attempts_total[5m])), rate(bifroest_connections_rejected_total[5m]) and rate(bifroest_http_rejections_total[5m]). increase(...[1h]) gives the corresponding hourly event count. Investigate sustained changes together with unauthenticated SSH connections, TLS aborts and audit-detail suppression; do not treat every 401/403 or unauthenticated HTTP asset fetch as a failed login.

The weighted active-session average is sum(bifroest_sessions_age_sum_seconds) / sum(bifroest_sessions_age_observations) when the denominator is greater than zero. Use oldest age to find outliers, but not as an inactivity timeout. Successful streaming channel lifetimes are deliberately absent from normal HTTP latency histograms.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Monitoring reference defines labels, measurement boundaries and TLS configuration.
  • Audit logs explains strict and best-effort failure policies.
  • Housekeeping describes retained sessions and conservative cleanup.

docs.title: OIDC login
docs.text: Sign in through your identity provider, then open a session with a normal SSH client or the WebUI. This example uses Authorization Code with PKCE and runs the session in Docker.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Linux Bifröst host service with access to Docker.
  • A domain pointing to Bifröst, with TCP port 443 reachable.
  • An OIDC provider and the sub claim of the user you want to allow.

docs.title: 1. Register the IdP client
docs.text:
Use these settings, substituting your own domain:

Setting Value Client type Confidential web client with a client ID and secret Grant Authorization Code with PKCE S256 Callback URL https://gateway.example.org/login/callback Token authentication client_secret_basic or client_secret_post Tokens ID token and refresh token

Enable your provider's refresh-token scope/settings. The example uses offline_access.

docs.title: 2. Configure Bifröst
docs.text:
Merge this into your host configuration. Replace the domain, ACME contact, issuer, credentials and allowed subject.

/etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
http:
  enabled: true
  domains: [ gateway.example.org ]
  tls:
    acme:
      enabled: true
      # Set this to true means you accept the terms of:
      # https://letsencrypt.org/repository/
      acceptTerms: true
      email: operator@example.org

flows:
  - name: oidc-shell
    discoverAsSlug: Shell
    http:
      requestUser: false
    requirement:
      http:
        includedSlug: '^Shell$'
    authorization:
      type: oidcAuthorizationCode
      issuer: https://idp.example.org/realms/company
      clientId: YOUR_CLIENT_ID
      clientSecret: YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
      scopes: [ openid, profile, offline_access ]
    environment:
      type: docker
      image: alpine
      user: "1000:1000"

      # Allows users with the field `shell` is equal to `true`
      # in their ID Token returned by the IdP to login.
      loginAllowed: '{{ eq .authorization.idToken.shell "true" }}'

(Re)start your Bifröst instance to active this configuration.

docs.title: Via SSH
docs.text:
ssh gateway.example.org 'id -u'
  1. Open the login link shown by your SSH client.
  2. Sign in at your IdP.
  3. Select your SSH client's two-character code from the browser's three choices to approve your own connection. A wrong choice or decline aborts the login.

The command should print 1000. Never approve a login link sent by someone else.

docs.title: Via WebUI
docs.text:
1. Open https://gateway.example.org/#Shell and choose OIDC.
  2. Sign in at your IdP in the automatically opened tab. If popups are blocked, use the displayed login link.
  3. The login tab closes automatically when possible. Return to the original tab to use the terminal; WebUI login has no SSH code selection.

Keep the original tab open; reloading it loses the pending login.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Need Change SSH only, with browser approval Keep global HTTPS enabled; set the flow's http.enabled to false. / then returns 404 if no HTTP-enabled flow remains. SSH without Bifröst HTTPS Enable Device Authorization at the IdP and use type: oidcDeviceAuth. Follow the IdP's verification instructions instead of the Bifröst approval step. Saved access Configure rememberMe. Session and refresh checks still apply.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Check Callback fails Registered callback URL, selected HTTP domain, port and TLS certificate No refresh token IdP client settings and required scopes IdP login succeeds, access denied Allowed sub and the environment's loginAllowed rule

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Authorization Code reference covers refresh checks and access-loss behavior.
  • Docker reference explains workload privileges and isolation.
  • Device Authorization reference covers the alternative flow without a Bifröst HTTP connection for SSH.

docs.title: Record, find and replay a session
docs.text: This Linux example adds audit logging and session recording to a local-account host. It generates real SSH command output, finds the sealed Recording through the CLI and replays it. Start with an installed Bifröst host and an allowed local account.

docs.title: Configure a recorded local-account flow
docs.text:
1. Add the auditlog and flow to the host configuration. This complete example uses the named default audit log:

    Bifröst host: /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
    auditlogs:
  default:
    recording:
      enabled: true

flows:
  - name: local
    authorization:
      type: local
    environment:
      type: local
      name: "{{.authorization.user.name}}"
      portForwardingAllowed: false

    The flow selects the explicitly defined default logger automatically; recording.enabled: true adds output recording. Without a defined default or explicit logger selection, neither runs. The default strict failure policy stops an affected task if local persistence fails. See audit configuration and Recording configuration.

  2. Restart Bifröst using the host's service manager. For a fresh installation, the default signing key, audit journal and Recording repository are created when enabled.

  3. Run a command through the workload SSH connection and let it finish:

    Workload terminal
    ssh alice@bifroest.example.org 'printf "recording-check\n"'

    Replace the account and host with your own. Bifröst records shell/command output; it does not capture raw keystrokes or SFTP and forwarding payloads. Forwarding is disabled in this example.

docs.title: Find and verify the generated Recording
docs.text:
1. On the Bifröst host, run inspection commands as the service user, with access to its configuration, signing key and repositories:

    Bifröst host
    bifroest recording ls default --limit=20

    The default Linux repository is /var/lib/engity/bifroest/recordings; the CLI verifies selected sealed originals in its sealed/ directory. If there are several entries, use their start times to find the test session; listing order is by Recording ID.

  2. Replace RECORDING_UUID with its ID and inspect and verify it:

    Bifröst host
    bifroest recording show default RECORDING_UUID --format=json
bifroest recording verify default RECORDING_UUID --require-full
bifroest audit verify default

    The configured signing identity supplies local producer trust. This clear Recording receives full verification without a decryption key.

docs.title: Replay or export its terminal output
docs.text:
1. Replay the Recording in the terminal:

    Bifröst host
    bifroest recording play default RECORDING_UUID --with-sensitive --speed=2

    The verified playback includes recording-check from the generated command.

  2. To save an asciicast v3 file instead, choose an existing private output directory outside managed storage:

    Bifröst host
    bifroest recording export default RECORDING_UUID \
  --with-sensitive \
  --output /srv/audit-evidence/session.cast

    Recording exports are complete, sensitive plaintext and are never redacted. Without an encryption recipient, signatures protect integrity but not confidentiality of the stored original either.

docs.title: Browser alternative
docs.text:
The same settings capture output from browser shells. With a management flow granting access.recordings.read and access.recordings.download:

  1. Choose Audit logs, select default, then open Recordings.
  2. Choose Open recording. For encrypted content, select your local recipient key and enter its passphrase to unlock it. Opening a Recording does not itself verify its signatures.
  3. Use Verify with an independently obtained producer ID to check signatures, then choose Play. The player's help button lists playback controls.

Decryption and playback run locally; the private key is not uploaded. See encrypted evidence for trust setup and browser compatibility for supported Recording sizes.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Manage a host remotely adds a separate administration flow and workstation alias.
  • Verify encrypted evidence on a workstation configures encryption and keeps private decryption keys off the server.
  • recording command reference documents all arguments, flags and execution modes.

docs.title: SSH gateway to an OpenSSH server
docs.text:
Connect with a regular SSH client to Bifröst and open a shell on a private OpenSSH server. Bifröst authenticates the incoming connection, then makes a separate SSH connection to the target. It is not a transparent proxy.

This Linux example requires a running Bifröst host service, an existing target-user account on target.example.org, and two distinct SSH keys: the client's key for Bifröst and Bifröst's key for the target.

docs.title: Prepare the two connections
docs.text:
1. Put the client's public key in /etc/engity/bifroest/gateway-clients.pub on the gateway. Keep the corresponding private key on the client.

  2. On the gateway, create a separate key for the target connection:

    sudo bifroest key generate \
   --identityFile /etc/engity/bifroest/id_target \
   --publicFile /etc/engity/bifroest/id_target.pub

    Add id_target.pub to target-user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the target. The private key stays on the gateway. 3. Verify the target host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel, then import that host key on the gateway:

    sudo bifroest key import host \
   --knownHostsFile /etc/engity/bifroest/target_known_hosts \
   --address target.example.org \
   --expectedFingerprint SHA256:REPLACE_WITH_VERIFIED_FINGERPRINT

    Do not use --expectedFingerprint unknown for a production target. The fingerprint must match the host key negotiated by this command.

docs.title: Configure Bifröst
docs.text:
Replace the host service's /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml with the following configuration, using your actual target address and account. Keep access to the gateway through another channel while changing its SSH service.

flows:
  - name: openssh-target
    authorization:
      type: simple
      rememberMe: allowedAndEnabledByDefault
      entries:
        - name: gateway
          authorizedKeysFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/gateway-clients.pub
    environment:
      type: ssh
      address: target.example.org:22
      user: target-user
      knownHostsFile: /etc/engity/bifroest/target_known_hosts
      identityFiles:
        - /etc/engity/bifroest/id_target
      portForwardingAllowed: false

Restart Bifröst (sudo systemctl restart bifroest.service), then connect from the client:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/YOUR_CLIENT_PRIVATE_KEY \
   gateway@gateway.example.org 'id -un'

The expected output is target-user. Check Bifröst's own host key with the gateway administrator on first connection; it is not the target's host key. No Bifröst account named gateway is needed: simple matches the incoming SSH name and its public key. If the target connection fails, first check the target account's authorized_keys and the verified knownHostsFile.

The example disables port forwarding. SFTP is allowed by default only if the target accepts it; the gateway does not forward arbitrary SSH session requests.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• SSH over HTTPS with OpenSSH and curl reaches the gateway without a direct SSH port.
  • Record, find and replay a session adds audit logging and session output recording.
  • SSH environment reference covers user certificates, Bifröst-to-Bifröst delegation, subsystems and forwarding policies.

docs.title: SSH over HTTPS with OpenSSH and curl
docs.text: Use your regular SSH client to reach Bifröst through HTTPS instead of a direct SSH port. SSH authentication, host-key verification, SFTP and forwarding policies remain unchanged.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Bifröst has HTTPS and its SSH tunnel enabled, with a trusted certificate and an SSH-eligible flow. A direct SSH listener and the WebUI are not required.
  • You have the flow's normal SSH credentials and the verified Bifröst SSH host-key fingerprint.
  • Your workstation has OpenSSH and a suitable curl build.

docs.title: Configure OpenSSH
docs.text:
Add this to ~/.ssh/config (%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\config on Windows), replacing HostName and User with your server and SSH login name:

Host bifroest-https
    HostName bifroest.example.org
    User alice
    ServerAliveInterval 30
    ServerAliveCountMax 3
    ProxyCommand curl -q -fsSN --no-progress-meter --http1.1 -T . -X POST -H "Expect:" -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" https://%h/api/v1/ssh

OpenSSH replaces %h with HostName. On Windows, use curl.exe instead of curl. Quote executable and file paths containing spaces.

For a private CA, add --cacert "/path/to/ca.pem" to ProxyCommand before the URL; do not disable certificate verification.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
ssh bifroest-https

Verify the SSH host key against the fingerprint provided by your administrator, then authenticate as usual. HTTPS certificate verification does not replace this SSH host-key check. The configured flow opens through the HTTPS tunnel; the keepalive settings keep idle connections active.

For file transfers, use the same configuration:

sftp bifroest-https

SFTP and port forwarding are available only when the selected environment and authorization allow them.

docs.title: Use WSS instead
docs.text:
Use a curl build with working WSS duplex support and replace only ProxyCommand:

    ProxyCommand curl -q -fsSN --no-progress-meter --http1.1 -T . -X GET -H "Expect:" wss://%h/api/v1/ssh

Warning

Windows curl 8.22.0/Schannel fails simultaneous WSS send/receive and can cause SSH integrity failures. Use the HTTPS/1.1 example above with that build.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• SSH gateway to an OpenSSH server routes authenticated sessions to a private SSH target.
  • OIDC login adds identity-provider authentication to SSH connections.
  • HTTP connection reference covers tunnel switches, TLS configuration and curl compatibility.

docs.title: Test a configuration
docs.text:
Suppose your configuration should send requests for ops to an SSH target. After authentication returns account alice, a rule should map her name to mapped-alice. A request for guest should match no flow.

This guide turns those expectations into tests. You need a Bifröst binary and a directory where you can create files. You do not need an SSH server, a running Bifröst service or an actual Alice account.

docs.title: What you are testing
docs.text:
You provide the rules and an invented situation; Bifröst calculates the result:

Part In this example Configuration Only ops matches flow primary; prefix the authenticated name with mapped-. Account facts Account alice exists for the test. Input Request ops; assume flow primary authenticated Alice. Calculated result Select primary and target user mapped-alice. Assertions Check that the returned decision, flow and names match.

Authentication is assumed, not performed. A selected result means the supported selection rules succeeded, not that a login or session succeeded. The scope reference describes exactly which rules are evaluated.

docs.title: 1. Choose the configuration
docs.text:
Test the same YAML file you intend to use when running Bifröst. You select it when invoking bifroest test, rather than copying it into the tests directory or fixing its path in a suite.

For this walkthrough, save the following example as configuration.yaml in your project directory. When adapting the guide to an existing configuration, use that file and adjust the test cases to its flows and rules instead.

configuration.yaml
flows:
  - name: primary
    requirement:
      includedRequestingName: '^ops$'
    authorization:
      type: local
      principal: 'mapped-{{ .authentication.principal }}'
    environment:
      type: ssh
      address: work.example.org
      user: '{{ .authentication.principal }}'
      acceptAllHostKeys: true
      portForwardingAllowed: false

The principal template adds mapped- to the authenticated name. The user template then uses that mapped principal as the SSH target user. These are Bifröst's normal YAML templates, not Lua expressions.

Offline example, not a deployment configuration

No connection to work.example.org is made. acceptAllHostKeys avoids requiring trust material in this fixture; do not copy that setting into a production gateway without proper target trust.

docs.title: 2. Describe the situation
docs.text:
Create a tests directory beside configuration.yaml and save tests/access_bftest.lua. Bifröst recognizes the _bftest.lua suffix. This file declares a suite called access with one test; it does not select a configuration file.

A few Lua conventions explain the example:

  • suite { ... } calls suite with a table. It is equivalent to suite({ ... }).
  • object { ... } supplies named data; list { ... } supplies ordered items.
  • verify = function(t, actual) ... end is called with the test context t and Bifröst's calculated result actual. t:IsEqual records a comparison.

The account below uses Linux/macOS facts. On Windows, apply the changes in Windows account facts before running it.

tests/access_bftest.lua
suite {
  name = "access",
  platform = { os = { "unix" } },
  environment = object {
    accounts = list { object { name = "alice", uid = 1001 } },
  },
  tests = {
    {
      name = "ops-selects-target",
      input = object {
        request = object { requestingName = "ops" },
        authentication = object {
          primary = object { outcome = "allow", account = "alice" },
        },
      },
      verify = function(t, actual)
        t:IsEqual("selected", actual.decision)
        t:IsEqual("primary", actual.flow)
        t:IsEqual("mapped-alice", actual.identity.principal)
        t:IsEqual("mapped-alice", actual.environment.user)
      end,
    },
  },
}

Here, authentication.primary refers to the YAML flow named primary. It does not refer to the suite name or the requested username. allow tells the test to assume that flow authenticated alice; it does not supply the expected final decision.

suite.environment describes the users available to the test. actual.environment describes the resulting SSH target. Despite the shared property name, those objects have different roles.

UID 1001 is invented test data, not an account to look up on your computer.

docs.title: Windows account facts
docs.text:
Change platform to { os = { "windows" } } and replace the account object with:

object { name = "alice", sid = "S-1-5-21-1-2-3-1001" }

The SID is also invented. No account needs to be created on Windows. This example selects an SSH target; the additional shell settings for a local Windows target are explained in Environment facts.

docs.title: 3. Run the test
docs.text:
From the directory containing configuration.yaml and tests, run:

bifroest test tests --configuration configuration.yaml

--configuration selects the YAML file to test. Its path is relative to your shell's working directory, not the suite directory. The suite contains only the test situations and assertions, so it can test the same file you later use for Bifröst without maintaining a separate configuration copy.

The command exits with status 0 and ends with:

RESULT: 1 PASSED, 0 FAILED, 0 SKIPPED

Use bifroest test tests --configuration configuration.yaml --verbose to see the suite and case name as well. An assertion mismatch returns 1; invalid input, an empty selection or a test execution/report error returns 2. See the command reference for flags and the full exit-code rules.

The CLI path is a fallback: an explicit suite.configuration takes precedence. Leave that property out when testing the configuration selected by the command. Dedicated, self-contained fixtures can still use it; see configuration selection.

docs.title: 4. Add an expected denial
docs.text:
Place this local variable before suite { ... } in the same file:

Denied test
local deniedRequest = {
  name = "guest-has-no-flow",
  input = object {
    request = object { requestingName = "guest" },
    authentication = object {},
  },
  verify = function(t, actual)
    t:IsEqual("deny", actual.decision)
  end,
}

Add deniedRequest, at the start of the suite's tests array, immediately before the existing { name = "ops-selects-target", ... } test table.

The guest request does not match ^ops$, so no flow attempts authentication. It needs no assumed authentication outcome. A denial is the expected result: the test passes because Bifröst denied the request.

Run again; the summary now shows two passes. To select only the first scenario:

bifroest test tests --configuration configuration.yaml --includes '^access/ops-'

docs.title: 5. See a failure and save CI results
docs.text:
Change the expected principal in the first test from mapped-alice to wrong-user. Its assertion now fails with a source line, expected/actual values and exit status 1. Restore the correct expectation afterward.

Save both machine-readable reports with:

bifroest test tests --configuration configuration.yaml --json reports/testing.json --junit reports/testing.xml

Let the exit status fail your CI step. Upload reports even after a failed step and use your CI's JUnit viewer for case names and failure details. Parent directories are created and existing regular reports can be replaced; see report files for protections and write-failure behavior. Use synthetic values: assertion details may appear in reports.

docs.title: Run in a container
docs.text: The same command is available in the normal Bifröst image. See the restricted container example for read-only inputs, non-root execution and report mounts.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem What to check No tests selected Filename suffix, filters and the binary's platform. A required account or field is unknown Supply it in the test facts; omission does not mean absence. The configuration cannot be loaded Check --configuration relative to your invocation directory; see configuration selection. A template is unsupported Check the supported template subset. Assertions pass, but exit status is 2 Check report paths and the filesystem cause on stderr.

docs.text:
• Look up Lua functions, Suites, Tests or result fields.
  • Model HTTP requests or OIDC data.
  • Browse the complete runnable examples.

docs.title: Source tree
docs.text: The repository follows the REUSE Specification. REUSE.toml, file headers and the license texts in LICENSES/ provide machine-readable copyright and license information for every tracked file. Pull requests and releases run reuse lint, and a failed check blocks the corresponding operation.

docs.title: Go dependencies
docs.text:
Every release build scans the Go modules actually linked into each Bifröst binary. The machine-readable policy in third-party-license-policy.json distinguishes:

  • license identifiers that are approved for automatic use;
  • license identifiers explicitly rejected by a reviewed policy decision; and
  • license identifiers that require manual review.

The policy currently approves Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC and MIT. It does not globally reject a license identifier. Every unclassified license requires manual review and fails the build until a reviewed decision is recorded. This avoids treating an unknown license as implicitly approved or rejected.

docs.title: Release artifacts
docs.text:
Release archives and container images include the project license, applicable license texts and an artifact-specific THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt. Companion SPDX 2.3 and CycloneDX 1.6 SBOMs identify the components found in each archive or image. The release manifest relates these files to their platform, edition and digest; see the compliance artifacts for the current release.

The Go dependency policy applies to modules linked into the Bifröst executable. Container image SBOMs additionally inventory packages inherited from the pinned base image. Their reported license metadata is preserved without inferring a Bifröst policy approval; NOASSERTION remains where upstream package metadata does not provide a conclusion.

The documentation build toolchain is not embedded in or distributed with Bifröst artifacts and is therefore outside this artifact license policy.

docs.title: Embedded browser components
docs.text: The browser includes third-party components under their respective licenses. Their license texts and notices are included with the release.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Bifröst does have the following important entities:

  1. Connection which is established by an SSH client or the HTTPS browser interface.

  2. Authorization are used to authorize the user and acquire more relevant information, needed for successful execution.

  3. Environment is the place where the user's session is executed in; the target shell where to user executes its tasks.

  4. The Session will be created for the user when the authorization was successful and an environment can be created. It is used to identify the current connection and any subsequent session.

  5. Bifröst can have one or more Flows. This can define different combinations of authorizations and environments based on different rules. This is comparable with Virtual hosting like HTTP server are already providing it for years.

  6. Configuration tests check how flow requirements, identity mapping and environment settings work together for a request. They use the same configuration you intend to deploy, with supplied authentication results and account facts. No login or session is started.
