docs.title: Templating
docs.text:
In many places of the configuration Bifröst can not only be customized by using static strings or numbers, but by using templates as well.

Bifröst uses the template engine of Go. A collection of rather good resources to learn can be found at HashiCrop's Nomand Developer documentation.

In the documentation of each Bifröst's component you may find the type the icon , followed by the corresponding context object (like Connection or Authorization). The result will be like:

  • Authorization
  • Connection

docs.title: Base types
docs.text: Each base type (string, bool, uint32, ...) has a different handling in edge cases.

docs.title: string
docs.text:
A template of type String is always rendered to a corresponding string - as it is.

Examples:

  • Foo{{ "Xyz" }}Bar or will result in FooXyzBar.
  • Foo{{ 123 }}Bar or will result in Foo123Bar.

docs.title: bool
docs.text:
A template of type Bool is always rendered into a boolean value (true or false). The following rules are evaluated to decide for either true or false:

  • false: If the value trimmed and converted to lower-cases is one of: false, disabled, 0, no, off, <empty>, nil or null
  • true: Everything else

docs.title: uint32
docs.text: A template of type uint32 is always rendered into an unsigned integer with 32 bits value (0 or more). An empty value is always assumed as 0.

docs.title: float32
docs.text: A template of type float32 is always rendered into a floating point number with 32 bits value (0.0 or more). An empty value is always assumed as 0.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A configuration test answers questions such as: “When Alice requests ops, does this configuration choose the expected flow and SSH target user?”

You supply a configuration and describe a situation. Bifröst evaluates its rules for that situation. Your test then compares the result with your expectations. For a step-by-step introduction, see Test a configuration.

docs.title: How a test works
docs.text:
Part What you provide or receive Configuration The YAML rules you want to test. Environment facts Users and groups that should exist, or be known not to exist, for this test. These are not read from your computer. Input A request and the authentication results the test should assume. Result The flow, identity and target settings calculated by Bifröst. Assertions Comparisons between that result and what you expected.

For example, the test can assume that authentication returned local account alice. It can then check that the configuration maps Alice's name to mapped-alice and chooses that user on an SSH target. It does not check Alice's password or connect to the target.

A suite groups tests that share configuration and environment facts. Save each suite in a file named *_bftest.lua, then run it with bifroest test.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Save the configuration you want to test as configuration.yaml:

configuration.yaml
flows:
  - name: primary
    requirement: { includedRequestingName: '^ops$' }
    authorization: { type: local }
    environment:
      type: ssh
      address: work.example.org
      user: alice
      acceptAllHostKeys: true

In the same directory, save the test suite as access_bftest.lua:

access_bftest.lua
suite {
  name = "access",
  environment = object {},
  tests = {
    {
      name = "guest-has-no-flow",
      input = object { request = object { requestingName = "guest" } },
      verify = function(t, actual)
        t:IsEqual("deny", actual.decision)
      end,
    },
  },
}

The configured flow matches only ops, so the guest request matches no flow. No account facts or authentication outcomes are needed. The test passes because the calculated denial matches the assertion. No connection to the SSH target is made; the SSH settings, including acceptAllHostKeys, are only fixture data.

From that directory, run:

bifroest test -c configuration.yaml .

-c selects the configuration file. . finds all *_bftest.lua files in the current directory and its subdirectories.

The result is 1 PASSED, 0 FAILED, 0 SKIPPED and exit status 0. For a positive selection example, continue with the guide.

docs.title: Lua reference
docs.text:
Use these pages to look up a function or data type while writing a test:

Reference Contains Functions and values suite, object, list, file_content, null and the small amount of Lua syntax you need. Suites Shared configuration, environment facts, the test list and platform selectors. Tests Individual test properties: name, input and verification function. Input Request and Authentication assumption properties. Requests SSH/HTTP request properties and method selection. Environment facts Account, group and explicit-absence properties. OIDC data OIDC identity, OAuth token, ID token and UserInfo properties. Test context The t argument passed to your verification function. Results The actual argument: decision, identity and target settings. Assertions t:IsEqual(expected, actual, reason?). Data types Shared value types such as Name, authentication modes, selectors and identifiers.

For command arguments and filters, use the CLI reference. For output formats, use Reports.

docs.title: Scope and limitations
docs.text:
The testing scope is post-authentication/session-target: configuration validation, SSH/HTTP flow selection, identity mapping, and SSH/local target settings. The local environment's loginAllowed rule is also evaluated. These use the same rules as the running service, within the supported template subset.

A selected target is not a successful login

actual.decision = "selected" means these selection steps succeeded. Authentication is assumed. Credentials, native account eligibility, target connections, sessions and effective runtime permissions have not been tested.

No service, HTTP listener, browser, IdP exchange, host-account lookup, provisioning or target process is started. HTTP endpoint checks such as TLS, domain allowlists and browser Origin/CSRF are outside this test. Token signatures and lifetimes are not verified. Authentication types and targets outside the supported local/OIDC and SSH/local combinations return errors when needed; they are not silently treated as denials.

An expected deny can be a passing test. Invalid configuration, missing required facts or unsupported behavior are errors, not a successful denial. See isolation and limits for available Lua features, resource bounds and the distinction from an OS sandbox.

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text: An assertion states what should be true about a test's result. Bifröst records each comparison and reports any mismatch with its source line and values. Call assertions inside the test's verify function, using the Test context supplied as t.

docs.title: t:IsEqual(expected, actual, reason?)
docs.text: Compare two values. Use the colon (:) to call this method on t.

docs.title: expected
docs.text:
Data value or nil

The value your test expects. Put it first so the failure report reads in the right direction.

docs.title: actual
docs.text:
Data value or nil

The value to compare, usually a field of the Result passed to verify.

docs.title: reason
docs.text:
string

An explanation included in a failure report, at most 256 bytes. Use it to say why the expectation matters. Do not put secrets in assertion values or reasons.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: true when the values match, otherwise false. A mismatch records a failure but does not stop the function, so subsequent assertions can also run. Ignoring the return value does not ignore the failure.

docs.title: Comparison rules
docs.text:
• Values must have the same type: integer 1 differs from float 1.0.
  • Strings and booleans compare exactly; strings are not normalized.
  • Objects compare their fields recursively; lists compare length, item types, values and order. Use object/list for composite expectations.
  • Explicit null differs from an omitted Lua nil value.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
An invalid call, unsupported value, overlong/non-string reason or exceeded assertion limit is an execution error. Catching it with pcall does not turn the test into a pass. A valid mismatch inside pcall also remains recorded.

Every selected test must execute at least one t:IsEqual assertion. Lua's ordinary assert(...) is not a recorded testing assertion and does not satisfy that requirement.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Use this function as a Test's verify property:

local function verify(t, actual)
  t:IsEqual("selected", actual.decision)
  t:IsEqual("mapped-alice", actual.environment.user, "Use the mapped SSH account")
end

When expecting a denial, check its decision without reading fields that only exist on selection:

local function verifyDenial(t, actual)
  t:IsEqual("deny", actual.decision)
end

See Results for field availability and Reports for the distinction between assertion failures, execution errors and platform skips.

docs.title: Test context
docs.text:
The runner calls your verification function with two arguments, t and actual. t gives access to the test's original data and assertion methods. actual is the separately calculated Result. You may use different argument names, but their positions have these meanings.

All data properties are read-only. Write expectations with the IsEqual method.

docs.title: input
docs.text:
Input

The original input supplied by this Test. For example, t.input.request.host keeps the spelling you wrote, whereas actual.request.host contains the canonical host used for matching.

docs.title: environment
docs.text:
Environment facts

The supplied suite facts: known users, groups and absences. This is not actual.environment, which describes the selected target settings.

docs.title: configuration
docs.text:
Test configuration

A small view of the loaded configuration, described below. It is not the whole YAML configuration and exposes no configuration secrets.

docs.title: Test configuration
docs.text: This is the value of t.configuration.

docs.title: flows
docs.text:
[]Test flow

The configured flows in configuration order. No authorizer or environment configuration objects are exposed through this view.

docs.title: Test flow
docs.text: Each entry in t.configuration.flows has one property:

docs.title: name
docs.text:
Flow Name

The configured flow name. For example, t.configuration.flows[1].name.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: t:IsEqual(expected, actual, reason?) compares values and records the result as an assertion.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The callback's basic shape is:

local function verify(t, actual)
  t:IsEqual("selected", actual.decision)
end

Inside a verification function for the first-test guide:

local function verify(t, actual)
  t:IsEqual("ops", t.input.request.requestingName)
  t:IsEqual("alice", t.environment.accounts[1].name)
  t:IsEqual("mapped-alice", actual.environment.user)
end

The three names are deliberately different: requested name, assumed account, and selected SSH target user.

docs.title: Reading values
docs.text: Use field access for objects and 1-based indexing or # for lists. Reading a missing named field is an error; it does not turn into a guessed value. There is no generic iteration over these read-only views. See Data value for data types and null/omission rules.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
These types describe values used by the Lua API, not classes to instantiate. Object properties are documented on their owning reference pages. Schema property names must use the exact documented spelling, including case; aliases such as UID for uid are rejected. Flow names and arbitrary OIDC claim and OAuth extra keys remain data keys, not schema properties. General Bifröst types, such as Flow Name, retain their normal meaning; a testing Name is a different type.

Fixture strings and object keys must be valid UTF-8. Malformed byte sequences are rejected before JSON conversion, not replaced or normalized. Valid Unicode, including an explicitly supplied replacement character (�), is preserved.

docs.title: Architecture selector
docs.text: A case-sensitive binary architecture identifier, such as amd64, arm64 or armv7. Its string form matches [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}. It selects the Bifröst binary, not the target or SSH client architecture.

docs.title: Authentication method
docs.text:
A string selecting the authentication path: password, keyboard-interactive or oidc. The permitted transport/authorizer combinations are documented under request method eligibility.

An omitted or explicitly empty request method uses password. That default does not enable OIDC. The calculated result always contains the effective method.

docs.title: Authentication mode
docs.text:
A string describing how an authentication assumption supplies an identity:

Value Meaning post-authentication Local authentication has already resolved the supplied account. mapped-local Evaluate the configured local remoteName, then bind that account. verified-oidc Use an explicitly supplied OIDC identity; verification is assumed.

Local assumptions default to post-authentication. Successful OIDC assumptions must explicitly select verified-oidc. Results contain the effective mode. See test input for the corresponding data.

docs.title: Authentication outcome
docs.text: allow assumes authentication succeeded; deny assumes it failed. This string is an input observation, not the expected overall Decision. Even after allow, flow matching, identity mapping and target rules must succeed.

docs.title: Data value
docs.text:
Type Meaning and example string Text, such as "alice". bool true or false. integer A whole-number Lua value, such as 1001. float A floating-point Lua value, such as 1.0; distinct from an integer in assertions. Object Named fields created with object { ... }. []T Ordered items of type T, created with list { ... }. null Explicit absence, only where permitted.

For example, []Account means a list of the Account objects documented in this reference. Values received through the test context and results use the same vocabulary and are read-only.

Lua nil is not an object field value: it omits the field. It can still be compared by IsEqual, for example after an out-of-range list read. It is distinct from explicit null. Ordinary Lua tables can build declarations and generate cases; use object/list for fixture data and composite assertions so their intended shape is explicit.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A calculated result string: selected when the supported selection steps succeeded, otherwise deny. There is no allow decision. Selection is not a login or complete access authorization; see scope.

docs.title: Name
docs.text:
A suite or test name, represented as a case-sensitive string of 1–80 Unicode code points. It accepts printable letters, numbers and combining marks, plus exactly .,-_[]()%@!~=+.

Whitespace, separators, quotes, controls, invisible format/default-ignorable characters, variation selectors, emoji and other symbols are rejected. Names are not Unicode-normalized or silently rewritten.

Examples: access, ops-selects-target, team[1]. The slash in access/ops separates two Names; it cannot be part of either Name. This type does not apply to configured flow names or account names.

Qualified suite/test names must be unique across platform-matching suites; mutually exclusive platform variants may share names. Filters use regular expressions, so escape metacharacters when matching names literally.

docs.title: OS selector
docs.text: A case-sensitive binary operating-system identifier, such as linux, darwin or windows. Its string form matches [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}. The selector-only group unix means exactly Linux and macOS. It selects the Bifröst binary and does not emulate another OS.

docs.title: Requesting name
docs.text:
The requested login name as a UTF-8 string, unchanged by matching. This is not a suite/test Name, an authenticated identity or a target account.

  • SSH: nonempty, not all whitespace, at most 128 bytes, without control characters.
  • HTTP: at most 256 bytes, without control characters. Nameless mode uses "" explicitly; the configured flow's requestUser rule determines whether a name is required.

Missing/null is not an empty name. Names are not trimmed.

docs.title: Server authority
docs.text:
A server host with an optional numeric port, represented as a string such as app.example.org:8443 or [2001:db8::1]:8443. Ports range from 1 to 65,535; IPv6 addresses require brackets. A scheme, user information, path, query or fragment is not accepted. This is an authority, not a URL or the remote client's host.

See request normalization for canonical host and HTTPS origin values. An omitted port means the default HTTPS port, 443.

docs.title: SID
docs.text: A canonically spelled Windows security identifier, represented as a string, for example S-1-5-21-1-2-3-1001. Account and group facts must use their actual respective identifiers within the fixture; display names are not SID aliases. Supplying a SID does not query or create a Windows account or group.

docs.title: Slug
docs.text: A case-sensitive string: "" for the root, or one/two segments separated by /, for example Work or servers/Work. Each segment contains 1–64 ASCII letters, digits or hyphens. The exact first segments login, assets and api are reserved. Leading/trailing slashes, empty segments and URL-encoded aliases are not accepted; the value is not URL-decoded.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: The request transport string: ssh or http. An omitted transport uses ssh; other values, including an explicitly empty string, are errors.

docs.title: Unix ID
docs.text: A Lua integer in the range 0–4,294,967,295, used for a Unix UID or GID. A float such as 1001.0 is not an integer ID. Windows SIDs are a separate type.

docs.title: UTC timestamp
docs.text: A string in RFC 3339 UTC form ending in Z, for example "2030-01-01T00:00:00Z". Non-UTC spellings are rejected. Raw OIDC exp/iat claims, when included, are interpreted as whole Unix seconds. The resulting instants must exactly match the metadata timestamps; matching only the seconds component of a fractional metadata timestamp is not enough.

docs.title: Version selector
docs.text:
A string matching the Bifröst binary's version:

Form Matches Complete SemVer, optionally prefixed with lowercase v Exact version including prerelease identity; build metadata does not affect equality. 1 or 1.2 Stable versions in that major/minor series, not prereleases. [1.3.5,1.4.0) Interval: square endpoints include, round endpoints exclude. One bound may be omitted with an open endpoint, e.g. (,1.4.0]. Bounds must be complete SemVer. development or another non-SemVer label Exact case-sensitive full string, without trimming or wildcards. Never matches a SemVer entry.

Empty/reversed intervals are invalid. Prereleases match an interval only when at least one bound contains a prerelease and the comparisons match. A string starting with [ or ( must be a valid interval, not an arbitrary label. Each selector is nonempty and at most 256 bytes.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Input describes the situation to test, not what you expect to happen. For example: someone requests ops, and authentication for flow primary returns account alice. Expectations belong in assertions.

Supply an object as the value of each test's input. The runner does not obtain missing observations from the host or an IdP.

docs.title: request
docs.text:
Request

The logical SSH or HTTP request. At least requestingName must be explicit.

docs.title: authentication
docs.text:
Object<Flow Name,Authentication assumption>

An object keyed by configured YAML flow name, not username or test name. Supply a result for every flow whose authentication the request needs to attempt. Omitting a needed result is an error, not an assumed denial.

If no flow reaches authentication, no outcomes are needed; object {} makes that explicit. Requirements may exclude a flow before its outcome is consulted.

docs.title: Authentication assumption
docs.text: Each value in input.authentication describes one flow's authentication assumption with the properties below. Bifröst does not check a password or run an OIDC exchange to obtain it.

docs.title: outcome
docs.text:
Authentication outcome

The authentication result to assume for this flow, not the expected overall test decision.

docs.title: mode
docs.text:
Authentication mode

How to interpret the assumption. Local authentication defaults to post-authentication; OIDC success requires explicit verified-oidc. See local mapping and OIDC data.

docs.title: account
docs.text:
string

Required for local allow in post-authentication mode. It names an existing supplied Account, not an account to look up on the host. Optional in mapped-local mode, but must agree with the resolved name when supplied. Do not supply it for OIDC.

docs.title: oidc
docs.text:
OIDC identity

Required for an OIDC allow with mode = "verified-oidc". Not accepted for local authentication or with an OIDC deny. The identity must match the configured flow's issuer.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Use this object as a test's input:

local input = object {
  request = object { requestingName = "ops" },
  authentication = object {
    primary = object { outcome = "allow", account = "alice" },
  },
}

primary refers to flows[].name: primary in the YAML. alice is a supplied account fact. Neither name is derived from the suite's name.

For an assumed authentication denial:

local outcomes = object {
  primary = object { outcome = "deny" },
}

Use outcomes as input.authentication. A denial can permit a later eligible flow to be tried. An evaluation error stops that path instead. For published HTTP assignments, see flow matching.

docs.title: Isolation and limits
docs.text:
Tests use the selected YAML configuration and the facts you supply. Lua can read additional fixture data only through file_content. Each case starts with fresh Lua state, so variables changed by a previous case do not affect it. Bifröst includes GoLua v0.4.1 (Lua 5.5); you do not need an external Lua installation. Builds without quota support refuse to run tests.

Not a hard OS sandbox

Interpreter accounting/cooperative time limits do not impose hard process RSS/CPU bounds or protect against interpreter defects and hostile concurrent filesystem changes. Use an outer OS/container boundary when needed.

docs.title: Lua capabilities
docs.text:
The Lua API provides suite, object, list, null, file_content and the allowlisted base functions assert, error, type, tostring, tonumber, pairs, ipairs, next, select, pcall.

There is no os, io, package, require, load, dofile, debug/Go bridge, raw access, metatable manipulation, random/clock library or print. Immutable views cannot be modified with raw setters/reflection. file_content captures data, not executable Lua includes. See file input rules.

pcall shares the outer budget, not a replenished child quota. Caught/ignored helper or assertion errors remain errors/failures; quotas cannot become success through exception handling.

docs.title: Resource bounds
docs.text:
Resource Limit Each discovery/replay, including compilation/verification 2,000,000 VM CPU units, 16-MiB allocation-accounting budget, 500-ms runtime quota. Each source/configuration/helper file 64 KiB. Captured file_content inputs per suite 64 paths, 4 MiB total. Discovery 100,000 inputs/directory entries, including ignored entries; 256 nested levels. Include/exclude filters At most 64 expressions per group, 4 KiB each. Suite/configuration 64 tests, 32 flows. Test data/assertions 128 assertions per test; 2,048 fixture nodes; depth 16; 4-KiB data strings. Platform selector 64 strings per field, 256 bytes each; OS/architecture identifiers at most 32 lowercase letters/digits, _/-. Admitted policy template 4-KiB source, 128 AST nodes, depth 16. Local target normalization 64 KiB, 2,048 nodes, depth 16, 4-KiB strings, retaining integer types.

Exceeding a bound is an error, not silent truncation or a skip. Comparison output is bounded; arbitrary runtime/provider errors and YAML content are not dumped. Assertion values/reasons can still appear in reports: use synthetic data.

docs.title: Policy templates
docs.text:
Lua quotas do not bound arbitrary Go template functions. Offline admission therefore permits only text, fields/literals, if/else and eq/ne/lt/le/gt/ge/and/or/not/len. Loops, named/recursive templates, variable/chain constructs and all other functions, including allocating Sprig helpers and host readers, are rejected.

Admitted expressions still use the production renderer, not a separate policy implementation. Local mapping and OIDC snapshots describe additional field/method boundaries.

docs.title: Configuration admission
docs.text: YAML aliases/merges are rejected before normal product decoding. Windows local environments require explicit host-dependent shell selectors before defaults can enter the controlled projection. Product packages may initialize globals at process startup, but they are not used for these selectors. Other defaults, references and validation remain production behavior.

docs.title: Container execution
docs.text:
The normal Bifröst image accepts the same test command. The container runtime starts it; Lua cannot create containers. Prepare a locally available image and existing absolute host directories first. Replace paths, LOCAL_IMAGE_ID and UID/GID with your local values. Mount the test directory and the same configuration file you intend to use for Bifröst, both read-only. The report directory must be writable by that user:

docker run --rm --pull=never --network=none --read-only --user 1000:1000 --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges --pids-limit=64 --memory=256m --cpus=1 --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,nodev,size=16m --mount type=bind,src=/absolute/project/tests,dst=/workspace/tests,readonly --mount type=bind,src=/absolute/project/configuration.yaml,dst=/workspace/configuration.yaml,readonly --mount type=bind,src=/absolute/reports,dst=/reports --workdir=/workspace LOCAL_IMAGE_ID test tests --configuration configuration.yaml --json /reports/testing.json --junit /reports/testing.xml

Inputs and the root filesystem are read-only; only reports and bounded temporary storage are writable. No network, published ports or host sockets are needed. These outer limits do not replace the Lua limits above. Linux container results do not establish native Windows/macOS behavior.

docs.title: Environment facts
docs.text:
Describe users and groups that should exist for the test. They do not need to exist on your computer. An account record, an assumed authentication result and a selected target user are separate things.

Use an object as suite.environment. Omitted observations are unknown, not automatically absent. If a rule needs an unknown account or metadata value, the test errors instead of looking it up on the host. Contradictory observations and wrong-platform facts are rejected. The binary's platform determines the account format; a platform selector does not emulate another OS.

docs.title: accounts
docs.text:
[]Account

Known existing accounts. Omission supplies no existing-account observations. Use list {} when none are needed. This does not declare every other name absent.

docs.title: absentNames
docs.text:
[]string

Names explicitly known not to exist. Absence by name does not invent an absence observation for an unrelated identifier.

docs.title: absentUIDs
docs.text:
[]Unix ID

Unix only. UIDs explicitly known not to exist.

docs.title: absentSIDs
docs.text:
[]SID

Windows only. Account SIDs explicitly known not to exist.

docs.title: localGroups
docs.text:
[]Windows local group

Windows only. Known local groups and their direct SID members, for management group checks. Account group metadata alone is not that membership evidence. No nested/domain membership expansion is performed.

docs.title: absentGroupNames
docs.text:
[]string

Windows only. Local group names explicitly known not to exist.

docs.title: Account
docs.text: Each entry in environment.accounts describes one known account. Optional metadata must be supplied when a tested rule reads it; nothing here requests account creation.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Account name. Windows requires a valid local SAM account name, not a domain or Microsoft Entra identity. Unix name comparison is case-sensitive; Windows account-name matching is case-insensitive.

docs.title: uid
docs.text:
Unix ID

Required on Unix; not accepted on Windows. The account UID.

docs.title: sid
docs.text:
SID

Required on Windows; not accepted on Unix. The account SID.

docs.title: displayName
docs.text:
string

Display name for rules that read it. There is no guessed name or host lookup.

docs.title: homeDir
docs.text:
string

Home/profile directory for rules that read it. Supplying a path does not read, create or load that directory/profile.

docs.title: shell
docs.text:
string

Shell metadata for rules that read it. No host shell default is consulted.

docs.title: group
docs.text:
Group

Unix only. Primary group. It is distinct from supplementary groups.

docs.title: groups
docs.text:
[]Group

Supplementary groups on Unix; direct local alias metadata on Windows. An omitted list is unknown. An explicit list {} is a known empty observation.

docs.title: Group
docs.text: An account's primary/supplementary group metadata, used in accounts[].group and accounts[].groups[]. Windows has no primary group in this model.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Group name; on Windows, a valid local SAM group name.

docs.title: gid
docs.text:
Unix ID

Required on Unix; not accepted on Windows. The group GID.

docs.title: sid
docs.text:
SID

Required on Windows; not accepted on Unix. The local group SID.

docs.title: Windows local group
docs.text: Each entry in environment.localGroups describes a group and its direct members.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Local group name; comparisons are case-insensitive.

docs.title: sid
docs.text:
SID

The group SID, distinct from an account SID in the same fixture.

docs.title: members
docs.text:
[]SID

The complete direct member SID list. It is required when a membership check needs it. Omission is unknown; list {} means no direct members. Matching uses SIDs, not display names.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Use this object as suite.environment on Linux/macOS:

local environment = object {
  accounts = list { object { name = "alice", uid = 1001 } },
  absentNames = list { "new-account" },
}

Use this list as suite.environment.localGroups on Windows:

local localGroups = list {
  object {
    name = "bifroest-managed", sid = "S-1-5-21-1-2-3-3001",
    members = list { "S-1-5-21-1-2-3-1001" },
  },
}

docs.title: Local account mapping
docs.text:
For a local authentication assumption, omitted mode or post-authentication means the account name is already resolved. It does not claim the configured remoteName or a native login ran.

mapped-local first evaluates the configured remoteName. Only .remote.user and supported literal/conditional expressions are available at that step; host, connection and credential fields are not supplied. An optional account must agree with the mapping. The resolved account must be a supplied existing Account for allow; unknown/absent accounts are errors. A mapped-local deny still evaluates the mapping before denying.

docs.title: Management membership
docs.text:
In configuration templates, .authorization.user.managed refers to the authenticated account and the chosen flow's managedGroup, not the target account. For Unix it compares names: a matching primary group needs no supplementary list; otherwise the supplementary groups must be known. Windows uses the direct SID membership observations above. A known absent management group produces the same negative result as the service.

Without a local environment, this template field is present with no value (nil), not false. Applicable but unknown membership is an error. See the Local User context for the production meaning; the test supplies its observations instead of reading them.

docs.title: Local target settings
docs.text:
Returned target fields are documented under Local target. The local loginAllowed rule is checked before target lookup or rendering; false produces decision = "deny", stage = "local-login". Missing facts or template failures remain errors. The SSH environment's loginAllowed rule is not evaluated by this scope.

For Windows local targets, every local environment in the loaded YAML must explicitly provide shellCommand and execCommandPrefix; empty lists are valid. This prevents host-dependent defaults from entering the test. See the Unix/Windows examples.

docs.title: Functions and values
docs.text: Bifröst supplies the functions on this page to every test file. You do not import a module or install Lua separately. For a complete first suite, see the guide.

docs.title: Reading the syntax
docs.text:
Lua uses { ... } to write a table of named properties or numbered items:

local account = { name = "alice", uid = 1001 }
local names = { "alice", "bob" }

local declares a variable. account.name reads a named property; names[1] reads the first item. Lua lists start at 1, not 0.

suite { ... } is a function call, not a special declaration language. Lua lets you omit parentheses when the only argument is a table: it means suite({ ... }). The same applies to object { ... } and list { ... }.

function(t, actual) ... end defines the verification function. The runner provides t and actual when it calls that function. The colon in t:IsEqual(...) calls a method on t; keep it when writing assertions.

docs.title: suite(definition)
docs.text: Register the tests in this file. Call it exactly once in every suite file.

docs.title: definition
docs.text:
Suite

An ordinary Lua table describing the suite. Its tests property contains ordinary Test tables; their input data uses object and list as below.

docs.title: Return value and errors
docs.text:
No return value. Invalid declarations or a second registration in the same file are errors, even if caught with pcall.

See the Suite properties and example.

docs.title: object(fields)
docs.text: Create a read-only object with named fields. Use it for test input, environment facts and object-valued expectations, including an empty object.

docs.title: fields
docs.text:
Lua table

String-keyed fields whose values are supported data values. Use list for arrays. Cycles, metatables and unsupported values are errors.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: A read-only object containing a copy of the supplied values. Changing the original table does not change the object. Writing to the returned object or reading a missing named field is an error.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local account = object { name = "alice", uid = 1001 }
local emptyObject = object {}

docs.title: list(items)
docs.text: Create a read-only ordered list. Use it when the distinction between an empty list and an empty object matters.

docs.title: items
docs.text:
Lua array

A table with consecutive integer keys starting at 1 and no gaps. Items must be supported data values. Named keys, cycles and metatables are errors.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: A read-only copy of the list. values[1] reads its first item and #values returns its length. An out-of-range integer index returns Lua nil. Generic pairs/ipairs iteration over these read-only views is not supported; those functions can still be used with ordinary Lua tables while generating tests.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local accounts = list { object { name = "alice", uid = 1001 } }
local emptyList = list {}

docs.title: file_content(path)
docs.text: Read a fixture file as text. Most suites use this to obtain their YAML configuration; the function does not load or execute Lua code.

docs.title: path
docs.text:
string

A relative path below the physical directory containing the suite file. It is not relative to your shell's working directory.

docs.title: Return value and errors
docs.text:
The file's contents as a string. An unreadable or nonregular file, absolute path, traversal, escaping symlink or exceeded file limit is an error. Relative internal symlinks are supported; absolute symlinks are rejected even if they point inside the directory. Caught read errors still fail the suite/test.

The first successful read of each path is reused for that suite's tests, including reads first made inside a verification function. A discovery symlink does not change the allowed physical directory. The in-memory Go runner has no suite directory and cannot use this function. See file limits.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: local configuration = file_content("configuration.yaml")

docs.title: null
docs.text:
A value for known absence, where a field accepts it. It is not a function. Lua nil removes a table field; null keeps an explicit value in the data.

local knownAbsent = object { token = null }
local unknown = object {}

For OIDC, the first object says the OAuth token is absent; the second supplies no information about it. A missing observation can fail a test when the rule needs it. Not every field accepts null: follow its property documentation.

docs.title: Data values
docs.text:
The Data value type defines the supported strings, numbers, booleans, objects, lists and null/omission rules. Shared types such as Name describe more specific values used by properties; they do not require you to instantiate a class.

Other functions, supported syntax and runtime bounds are documented under isolation and limits.

docs.title: OIDC data
docs.text:
An OIDC test supplies the identity and data that authentication should be assumed to have returned. You can then test rules such as principal mapping from preferred_username. You do not supply a signed token or contact an IdP.

Use this object as the oidc property of a successful authentication assumption, with mode = "verified-oidc". The name means verification is assumed, not performed by the test runner. Token, ID token and UserInfo are independent: no data is copied between them or inferred from the requesting name.

See OIDC authorization for product configuration and request methods for SSH/HTTP eligibility.

docs.title: issuer
docs.text:
URL

The HTTPS issuer. It must exactly match the configured flow's issuer after supported template evaluation. An unrelated issuer is an error.

docs.title: subject
docs.text:
string

The assumed authenticated subject (sub). This starts as the identity's principal; configured principal mapping can change the principal, not this subject.

docs.title: token
docs.text:
OAuth token or null

The OAuth token data. Supply an object when the rule needs token fields, or null for known absence. If omitted, token data is unknown and errors when read.

docs.title: idToken
docs.text:
ID token or null

The verified ID-token data to assume. When retrieveIdToken is enabled, the observation must be supplied even if principal mapping does not read it. See visibility and absence for when null is accepted.

docs.title: userInfo
docs.text:
UserInfo or null

The UserInfo data to assume. Enabled retrieveUserInfo requires an object: null is not a successful retrieval. With retrieval disabled, omission can leave this data unknown.

docs.title: OAuth token
docs.text: If an object is supplied, all properties below are required, including empty strings or an empty extra object where appropriate. This is a data record, not an encoded token. For policy access, see OIDC Token context.

docs.title: accessToken
docs.text:
string

Synthetic access-token value.

docs.title: tokenType
docs.text:
string

Token type, for example Bearer.

docs.title: refreshToken
docs.text:
string

Synthetic refresh-token value; use "" when empty. No refresh is performed.

docs.title: expiry
docs.text:
UTC timestamp

Assumed expiry metadata. It is not checked as proof of token validity.

docs.title: extra
docs.text:
Object

Complete OAuth extra fields. Missing keys have the product's absent-value behavior rather than being invented. Use object {} for no extra fields.

docs.title: ID token
docs.text: All properties below are required when an object is supplied. The data describes an assumed verified token, not a JWT to verify. Policy access follows the OIDC ID Token context.

docs.title: issuer
docs.text:
URL

Must agree with the OIDC identity's issuer.

docs.title: subject
docs.text:
string

Must agree with the OIDC identity's subject.

docs.title: audience
docs.text:
[]string

The assumed audience list. Supplying it does not verify an actual token's audience.

docs.title: expiry
docs.text:
UTC timestamp

Assumed expiry time.

docs.title: issuedAt
docs.text:
UTC timestamp

Assumed issue time.

docs.title: nonce
docs.text:
string

Nonce metadata; supply "" explicitly when empty.

docs.title: accessTokenHash
docs.text:
string

Access-token hash metadata; supply "" explicitly when empty.

docs.title: claims
docs.text:
Object

The complete claims map. For example, a preferred_username claim can be used by the configured principal template. Use object {} when no raw claims are needed.

docs.title: UserInfo
docs.text: All properties below are required when an object is supplied. See OIDC User Info context for policy access.

docs.title: subject
docs.text:
string

Must agree with the OIDC identity's subject.

docs.title: profile
docs.text:
string

Profile value; supply "" explicitly when empty.

docs.title: email
docs.text:
string

Email value; supply "" explicitly when empty.

docs.title: emailVerified
docs.text:
bool

Assumed email-verification state. false is a value, not an omitted observation.

docs.title: claims
docs.text:
Object

The complete UserInfo claims map, separate from ID-token claims.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This is a value for input.authentication, not a complete suite. It assumes the configured flow is named primary, uses the issuer below and enables retrieveIdToken while disabling retrieveUserInfo:

local authentication = object {
  primary = object {
    outcome = "allow",
    mode = "verified-oidc",
    oidc = object {
      issuer = "https://issuer.example.org",
      subject = "id-123",
      token = null,
      idToken = object {
        issuer = "https://issuer.example.org",
        subject = "id-123",
        audience = list { "example-client" },
        expiry = "2030-01-01T00:00:00Z",
        issuedAt = "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z",
        nonce = "",
        accessTokenHash = "",
        claims = object { preferred_username = "alice" },
      },
    },
  },
}

For a complete runnable configuration and suite, see the OIDC examples.

docs.title: Visibility and absence
docs.text:
The product's retrieveIdToken/retrieveUserInfo settings determine which data configuration templates can read. Supplying a hidden record does not make it visible. Hiding a record does not change the authenticated issuer or subject.

null for an ID token is permitted with refresh enabled, but fails when retrieveIdToken is true and both refresh and forced-disposal verification are disabled. UserInfo retrieval always needs an object when enabled. An absent OAuth token is known absent; its token fields have no value in policy templates.

The result exposes the identity and authentication binding, not token/claim dumps. Principal mapping changes only the principal.

docs.title: Consistent values and types
docs.text:
Metadata and any duplicate standard claims must agree. For example, a raw sub claim cannot contradict subject, even when the record is hidden. Do not duplicate standard claims unless your test needs them.

Claims and extra fields use the same JSON-derived types as production policy templates. In particular, numeric claims are floating-point values: compare them with 1.0, not integer 1, in a Go template. This does not change the integer/float distinction in the original Lua input. Canonical metadata and aliases such as accessToken/access_token follow the linked context references.

docs.title: Timestamps in templates
docs.text: Metadata times use the UTC timestamp type. Configuration templates receive time values with the supplied UTC zone. Host-local formatting is not reproduced. Time method chains such as .expiry.Local or .issuedAt.Location are unsupported. Read specific data fields, not entire token objects; see template limits.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: Text, JSON and JUnit use the same completed result without reevaluating policy or assertions. Process status is defined by bifroest test. An expected denial can be a passing test. An assertion mismatch remains a failure, even when used deliberately to demonstrate reporting.

docs.title: Packages and ordering
docs.text:
Each physical directory containing suite candidates is a package. Explicitly provided empty directories also appear. A single tests/foo_bftest.lua belongs to tests; nested directories such as tests/team are separate packages, not rolled into their parent.

Paths use forward slashes and are relative to the physical invocation directory when possible. Symlinks retain physical identity and deduplication. Presentation follows positional-root order, then directory order; source execution remains sorted by canonical path.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
The default shows failing/error cases and one summary per package:

=== RUN   deliberately-red-unix/wrong-target-contract
red-unix_bftest.lua:19: expected "not-alice", actual "mapped-alice"; reason "Deliberately red smoke test"
--- FAIL: deliberately-red-unix/wrong-target-contract (0.001s, 1 assertion)
FAIL    pkg/test/examples/ssh (0.004s, assertions: 1, passed: 0, failed: 1, skipped: 3)

RESULT: 0 PASSED, 1 FAILED, 3 SKIPPED

-v / --verbose shows package, suite and test headers and every outcome, indented four spaces per level. For example, running the OIDC examples:

=== RUN   pkg/test/examples/oidc
    === RUN   assumed-oidc
        === RUN   device-mapped-identity
        --- PASS: device-mapped-identity (0.001s, 9 assertions)
        === RUN   code-mapped-identity
        --- PASS: code-mapped-identity (0.001s, 9 assertions)
    --- PASS: assumed-oidc (0.004s, assertions: 18, passed: 2, failed: 0, skipped: 0)
--- PASS: pkg/test/examples/oidc (0.004s, assertions: 18, passed: 2, failed: 0, skipped: 0)

RESULT: 2 PASSED, 0 FAILED, 0 SKIPPED

Times and source lines above illustrate the format; real locations follow the current source. Names are unquoted. Assertion locations use filename and Lua line; in-memory input uses <memory>:LINE. JSON retains full source paths. Text is rendered after the run completes, not streamed as live test events.

docs.title: Counts and empty packages
docs.text:
The final result counts tests, not assertions or suite headers. SKIPPED counts every declared test in a platform-excluded suite, before name filtering. Name exclusions do not count as skips. Loading/runtime/selection errors add ERRORS when nonzero; suite/package summaries also append errors: N.

Empty packages print SKIP package: no tests found; fully name-filtered packages say no tests selected. Neither creates passes or declared skips. A mixed run can pass if other tests ran, but an entirely empty/excluded selection still returns 2 and prints an explicit error.

Warnings/operational diagnostics go to stderr. Completed reports do not emit a redundant generic executable error log. Real invocation, report-write and independent cleanup failures remain visible.

docs.title: Measured durations
docs.text: The Go runner measures wall time once, outside Lua; text shows three decimal places. Tests include fresh VM/replay/evaluation/verification, suites include loading/configuration, and packages sum time spent on their own sources, not descendants. Total time additionally includes discovery. Serialization is excluded. No Lua clock is exposed and no execution duration is invented for platform-excluded tests. JSON durationSeconds and JUnit time use the same observations.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
--json PATH writes the shared report model:

Field Meaning apiVersion, scope Report format version and limited offline boundary. Suite declarations do not contain an apiVersion. packages, suites Physical package identity and suite/source metadata, including declared test counts. results Per-test package, suite, source, name, status, assertion count, failure details and categorized errors. durationSeconds Measured run/package/suite/test time where available. warnings Source warnings, separate from test errors. skippedSuites Excluded suites, their reason, declared tests and testNames. summary passed, failed, skipped, errors test counts. suite Singular name only when exactly one suite registered.

Platform exclusions are not passing result records. An empty selection adds a summary error even if all declarations were platform-excluded.

docs.title: JUnit XML
docs.text:
--junit PATH writes a testsuites root. Suites are grouped by physical source path and suite name. Cases keep their declared names; counts represent tests, not assertions.

  • Passed cases have no status child. Assertion failures use one failure type="assertion" containing all failures, expected/actual values, optional reasons and source/line. Execution/loading errors use error with the retained category and prior assertions in its body. A case never has both.
  • file retains the source path; line, when known, is the first assertion failure. Other locations remain in the body. Unknown locations, absent timings/timestamps and in-memory filenames are not invented.
  • Platform exclusions produce skipped with actual declared names/reason before name filters. An empty selection additionally emits no-tests-selected as an error. Warnings are preserved in system-err.
  • Properties include apiVersion, scope, authenticationAssumed=true, source and measured suites' physical package. This is not proof of authentication or complete authorization.
  • Markup is escaped. XML 1.0-forbidden code points/invalid UTF-8 are spelled out as \u… / \x…, not silently replaced.

For the separate Go reporting API, see the package documentation.

docs.title: Report files
docs.text:
Existing regular report files may be replaced, and missing parents are created. Symlinks, nonregular destinations, suite filenames, captured inputs and their aliases remain protected. JSON/JUnit destinations must differ.

The CLI writes text, then JSON, then JUnit; this is not a multi-file atomic transaction. A later failure returns 2 and leaves earlier reports intact. Each file is serialized privately beside its target, then renamed into place; serialization/close failure leaves an old destination intact and temporary files are cleaned up. The diagnostic keeps the report path and original cause. This is not a crash-durability or hostile-filesystem sandbox guarantee.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
A Request describes what someone is asking Bifröst to open. It supplies the name used by flow requirements and, for HTTP, the server authority and published slug. It is not an authenticated identity or a network connection.

Use an object as input.request.

docs.title: requestingName
docs.text:
Requesting name

The requested login name, for example ops. It is not automatically the authenticated account or the target user.

docs.title: transport
docs.text:
Transport = "ssh"

The logical transport whose flow-selection rules should be used.

docs.title: method
docs.text:
Authentication method = "password"

The authentication method whose configured rules should be used. The supported combinations are listed below. An explicit empty string also uses password; it does not enable OIDC.

docs.title: host
docs.text:
Server authority

Required for HTTP; not accepted for SSH. The Bifröst server authority. Supply it explicitly; there is no separate origin override.

docs.title: slug
docs.text:
Slug

Required for HTTP; not accepted for SSH. The requested published flow path. Use "" explicitly for the root.

docs.title: SSH
docs.text:
Use this object as input.request:

local request = object { requestingName = "ops" }

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
local request = object {
  transport = "http",
  requestingName = "ops",
  method = "oidc",
  host = "APP.Example.Org.:08443",
  slug = "servers/Work",
}

This describes a request to the HTTPS endpoint app.example.org:8443; it does not send an HTTP request. For the service's real endpoint behavior, see HTTP connections.

docs.title: Authentication methods
docs.text:
Method SSH HTTP password Local assumptions; OIDC rejects this method. Local assumptions; OIDC rejects this method. keyboard-interactive Local or either OIDC grant. Device Authorization or an eligible local interactive method, not Code Grant. oidc Unsupported input (error). Code Grant, when the configured callback origin matches the request origin.

Method eligibility still follows configuration and binary capabilities, including whether local interaction/PAM is available. A local assumption does not bypass those method-selection rules or run a native login.

If a method is ineligible, that flow's assumed result is not consumed. For example, a password request does not use an OIDC allow. Another eligible flow may be tried according to normal matching rules.

docs.title: Canonical request values
docs.text:
Your original values remain in t.input.request. actual.request shows the values used after matching normalization. In the HTTP example above:

Result field Value actual.request.host app.example.org actual.request.origin https://app.example.org:8443 actual.request.slug servers/Work

Origin is derived from authority. Host casing, IDNA, trailing DNS dots, IPv6 spelling, numeric port aliases and the default HTTPS port are canonicalized. Invalid authorities, slugs and encodings fail before an authentication outcome is used. Server authority does not supply .remote.host in policy templates.

See Request result properties for the returned data type.

docs.title: Matching and published flows
docs.text:
Requests use the same flow requirements, ordering and transport switches as the service. HTTP requestUser: true requires a non-whitespace name; false requires exactly "". Requirements still apply to nameless requests.

On a matching canonical host, a flow's discoverAsSlug fixes the request's published assignment. Failed requirements, incompatible name/method/origin, denial or error do not redirect that assignment to a generic flow. Root and valid unpublished slugs use ordinary configuration-order matching, denial fallback and error abort. Case-distinct slugs are not aliases.

The HTTP endpoint is assumed to have accepted the request. TLS/domain/browser checks are outside the testing scope. See the HTTP examples for complete suites.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
actual is the result calculated for one test. It is not the input echoed back and not a live session. Read it inside verify and compare fields with t:IsEqual. All fields are read-only; the decision controls which other fields exist:

Outcome Available data Flow/target selected Common fields, flow, identity, authentication and target settings. No flow accepted Common fields only. Local loginAllowed denied Common fields, flow, identity and stage = "local-login"; no target or authentication result. Evaluation error A report error, not an invented Result passed to verify.

Reading a field that is absent for this outcome is an error, not a nil return. Choose assertions for the outcome being tested rather than probing success-only properties after a denial.

docs.title: decision
docs.text:
Decision

Whether the supported selection steps selected a target or denied the request.

docs.title: scope
docs.text:
string

Always post-authentication/session-target.

docs.title: authenticationAssumed
docs.text:
bool

Always true: authentication outcomes were supplied by the test.

docs.title: request
docs.text:
Request result

The request values used for matching, after normalization.

docs.title: flow
docs.text:
Flow Name

The selected configured flow name. Also present for local-login denial; absent when no flow accepted the request.

docs.title: identity
docs.text:
Identity

The identity after configured principal mapping, present on selection or local-login denial.

docs.title: authentication
docs.text:
Authentication result

The authentication identity used on selection, before principal mapping. This is distinct from the target account and absent on denials.

docs.title: environment
docs.text:
SSH target or Local target

Calculated target settings on selection. Unlike t.environment, this is not the list of supplied account facts.

docs.title: stage
docs.text:
string

local-login when the local loginAllowed rule denied. Absent otherwise.

docs.title: Request result
docs.text: The request values used for matching, after normalization. Compare this with t.input.request when testing normalization. It is not a live Connection context. It has the following properties:

docs.title: requestingName
docs.text:
Requesting name

The requesting name, unchanged; not an authenticated principal.

docs.title: transport
docs.text:
Transport

The effective request transport.

docs.title: method
docs.text:
Authentication method

The effective method, including the password default when omitted in input.

docs.title: host
docs.text:
Host

HTTP only: canonical host without port.

docs.title: origin
docs.text:
URL

HTTP only: canonical HTTPS origin, including a nondefault port.

docs.title: slug
docs.text:
Slug

HTTP only: case-sensitive slug, including "" for the root. See request normalization.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: The identity after configured principal mapping, present on selection or local-login denial. These are the three returned data fields, not the entire production Authentication context:

docs.title: principal
docs.text:
string

The mapped principal. It is not automatically the target account.

docs.title: issuer
docs.text:
string

The identity's authority: local for local accounts, or the OIDC issuer.

docs.title: subject
docs.text:
string

UID/SID as a string for local accounts, or the assumed OIDC subject. Mapping the principal does not change issuer or subject. See the product's identity explanation.

docs.title: Authentication result
docs.text: The authentication identity used on selection, before principal mapping. This is distinct from the target account and absent on denials. Unlike the flow-keyed input assumptions, this object has the following properties:

docs.title: mode
docs.text:
Authentication mode

The effective mode that supplied the selected identity.

docs.title: account
docs.text:
string

Local modes only: the canonical bound account name, before principal mapping.

docs.title: remoteName
docs.text:
string

Mapped-local only: the name produced by the configured remoteName expression.

docs.title: issuer
docs.text:
URL

OIDC only: the assumed issuer.

docs.title: subject
docs.text:
string

OIDC only: the assumed subject. Neither tokens nor raw claims are returned here.

docs.title: Target types
docs.text: The selected configuration determines which shape below is returned. Values are settings, not evidence that a target exists or a connection/login succeeds. Forwarding settings are not a complete permission evaluation.

docs.title: SSH target
docs.text: See SSH environment configuration for the corresponding product settings. This shape has these properties:

docs.title: type
docs.text:
string

Always ssh.

docs.title: address
docs.text:
Net Address

Rendered and normalized address, including port, e.g. work.example.org:22.

docs.title: user
docs.text:
string

Rendered target account name, e.g. mapped-alice.

docs.title: portForwardingAllowed
docs.text:
bool

Rendered forwarding setting.

docs.title: reversePortForwardingAllowed
docs.text:
bool

Rendered reverse-forwarding setting.

docs.title: Local target
docs.text: The local environment returns common settings plus platform-specific account/group selectors. A name-based selector does not automatically acquire the supplied account's current UID/SID. Known absence can still produce settings for deferred provisioning; the test never provisions. The common properties are:

docs.title: type
docs.text:
string

Always local.

docs.title: kind
docs.text:
string

local-unix or local-windows.

docs.title: shellCommand
docs.text:
[]string

Rendered shell command arguments.

docs.title: execCommandPrefix
docs.text:
[]string

Rendered command prefix arguments.

docs.title: directory
docs.text:
string

Rendered working directory. The path is not opened or created by the test.

docs.title: portForwardingAllowed
docs.text:
bool

Rendered forwarding setting.

docs.title: account
docs.text:
Unix account selector

Unix only. Requested account settings, not a copy of Account facts. Integer IDs are preserved. Its properties are listed with the selector types below.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Windows only. Rendered/resolved target account name.

docs.title: requestedSID
docs.text:
SID or empty string

Windows only. Requested SID selector. An empty string is not an assertion of the current SID.

docs.title: displayName
docs.text:
string

Windows only. Rendered display-name setting.

docs.title: skel
docs.text:
string

Windows only. Rendered skeleton setting, not a directory copied by the test.

docs.title: groups
docs.text:
[]Windows group selector

Windows only. Rendered requested groups; not the current account membership list.

docs.title: Unix account selector
docs.text: The local Unix target's account object has the following properties:

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Requested/resolved account name. Name precedence and UID 0 follow the product resolver.

docs.title: uid
docs.text:
Unix ID or null

Requested UID, or null when no UID was requested.

docs.title: displayName
docs.text:
string

Rendered display-name setting.

docs.title: group
docs.text:
Unix group selector

Requested primary group.

docs.title: groups
docs.text:
[]Unix group selector

Requested supplementary groups.

docs.title: shell
docs.text:
string

Rendered shell setting.

docs.title: homeDir
docs.text:
string

Rendered home directory setting.

docs.title: skel
docs.text:
string

Rendered skeleton setting. No account or filesystem changes are performed.

docs.title: Unix group selector
docs.text: Used by the local Unix account selector's group and groups properties.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Requested group name.

docs.title: gid
docs.text:
Unix ID or null

Requested GID, or null if none was requested.

docs.title: Windows group selector
docs.text: Used by the local Windows target's groups property.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
string

Requested group name.

docs.title: gid
docs.text:
SID or empty string

Requested SID-valued group identifier. The name gid follows the product's Windows selector vocabulary; it is not a numeric Unix GID.

docs.title: Denial example
docs.text:
For an expected general denial, do not read success-only fields:

local function verify(t, actual)
  t:IsEqual("deny", actual.decision)
end

docs.title: Suites
docs.text: A suite groups tests sharing a YAML configuration and environment facts. Register it with suite(definition) in a file named *_bftest.lua. Each entry in tests is a Test; the suite's Platform object is documented on this page.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
Name

The suite's name in reports and filters.

docs.title: configuration
docs.text:
string

Optional YAML content, not a filename. Omit it to test the file selected by bifroest test --configuration PATH or the normal configuration fallback. Use this property for a suite that deliberately has its own fixture, for example file_content("configuration.yaml") reading beside the suite. Explicit content takes precedence over the CLI fallback. Empty or invalid content is an error, not a request to try a different source; see configuration selection.

docs.title: environment
docs.text:
Environment facts

An object describing known users, groups and absences. These are test facts, not an environment backend to start. Use object {} if no facts are needed.

docs.title: tests
docs.text:
[]Test

An ordinary Lua array of 1–64 test tables with consecutive keys starting at 1. Each entry supplies an input and a function that checks the calculated result. Use { ... }, not the read-only list helper, for this declaration array.

docs.title: platform
docs.text:
Platform

A table restricting this suite to particular Bifröst binaries. Omission imposes no restriction; see the Platform properties.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
A plain Lua table selecting Bifröst binaries, not targets or SSH clients. The CLI uses its own build metadata and has no platform override flags.

Alternatives within one property are OR-combined; supplied properties are AND-combined. Omitted properties match everything; an explicit empty array matches nothing. Each array accepts at most 64 selectors.

docs.title: os
docs.text:
[]OS selector

Binary operating systems to match, for example linux, darwin or the group unix.

docs.title: arch
docs.text:
[]Architecture selector

Binary architectures to match, for example amd64 or arm64.

docs.title: version
docs.text:
[]Version selector

Binary versions to match, for example 1.2, [1.3.5,1.4.0) or development.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
This is a complete suite for the configuration in the first-test guide. Save it under tests, then run bifroest test tests --configuration configuration.yaml from the directory containing that configuration file:

tests/reference_bftest.lua
suite {
  name = "ssh-target",
  platform = { os = { "unix" } },
  environment = object {
    accounts = list { object { name = "alice", uid = 1001 } },
  },
  tests = {
    {
      name = "selected-user",
      input = object {
        request = object { requestingName = "ops" },
        authentication = object {
          primary = object { outcome = "allow", account = "alice" },
        },
      },
      verify = function(t, actual)
        t:IsEqual("selected", actual.decision)
        t:IsEqual("primary", actual.flow)
      end,
    },
  },
}

To restrict platform further, use a table such as:

local supportedBinaries = {
  os = { "unix" },
  arch = { "amd64", "arm64" },
  version = { "1.2", "development" },
}

Use supportedBinaries as the value of suite.platform.

docs.title: Configuration fallback
docs.text:
For each suite, use the first applicable source:

  1. Its configuration content, when supplied.
  2. --configuration PATH, relative to the invocation directory.
  3. The normal platform configuration file.

The flag is a fallback, not an override. An unreadable/invalid chosen source fails instead of trying the next one. The shared fallback is read at most once, only when a selected test needs it. Loading starts no service or provider.

For the separate rules governing file_content, see the function reference.

docs.title: Platform skips and declaration errors
docs.text:
A mismatch skips all declared tests in the suite before name filtering. It is not a pass; an entirely empty/excluded run still returns 2. Lua declarations must compile and register valid suites on every platform. In particular, file_content(...) in a declaration still reads its file. Selectors do not hide syntax, helper, schema or quota errors.

Unknown suite/test properties are errors. Lua helpers and generated arrays are supported, but test groups and executable module/file includes are not. Excluded suites do not load/validate YAML, read a configuration fallback, evaluate rules or call verify. Limits are listed separately.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: A test is one entry in a suite's tests array. It describes one situation through input and checks Bifröst's calculated result through verify. The suite supplies the shared configuration and environment facts.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
Name

The case's name, unique within its suite. Reports and CLI filters use suite.name/test.name.

docs.title: input
docs.text:
Input

An object describing the request and assumed authentication outcomes for this case. It does not contain the expected result; assertions supply that.

docs.title: verify
docs.text:
function(t, actual)

A Lua function receiving Test context as t and Result as actual. Run at least one t:IsEqual assertion. Its return value is ignored.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This test uses the configuration and account facts from the first-test guide. Define it before suite { ... }:

Test definition
local selectedUser = {
  name = "selected-user",
  input = object {
    request = object { requestingName = "ops" },
    authentication = object {
      primary = object { outcome = "allow", account = "alice" },
    },
  },
  verify = function(t, actual)
    t:IsEqual("selected", actual.decision)
    t:IsEqual("mapped-alice", actual.environment.user)
  end,
}

Use tests = { selectedUser } in the suite, or add selectedUser, to its existing tests array.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text: Each selected test starts with a fresh Lua VM and replays the suite declaration. Globals and captured local variables therefore do not carry state from a previous test. Write declarations that produce the same inputs on each replay.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Bifröst is available as a binary for many different platforms, or even as an OCI/Docker image.

For OIDC login, an SSH gateway or session recording, see the task guides.

For production and HA deployments, see the operating model and availability guide: TCP load balancing, instance-local state and recovery.

Before we get started, you need to choose your operating mode. Here are the main differences to help you decide:

Criteria On Host In Docker/Container Available features All (depending on used edition) All (depending on used edition) Compatibility (os/architecture) Available for the most amount of different platforms. Available for the major platforms. Consumption (CPU/RAM/storage) Lowest possible consumption. Meaningful overhead, caused virtualization and additional processes. Host integration It runs directly on the host and has therefore direct access to everything on the host. If running in privileged mode and all required devices are mounted, same as On host. Host isolation Depends on service privileges and host configuration. Depends on container privileges, mounts and runtime access; a Docker socket grants broad host control. Interactions with containers Full, except if interacting with Docker for Desktop. Full Installation effort Minimal Minimal

If you're still not sure that to pick, maybe our Use-Cases will help you.

docs.text:
Different guides, for the different ways how to operate Bifröst:

  1. On Host
  2. In Docker/Container

docs.text: Read Use-Cases and the configuration documentation to see what you can do more with Bifröst.

Bifröst is available in different distributions.

On this page you'll find:

docs.title: Operating Systems
docs.text: Bifröst is currently available for Linux, macOS and Windows.

docs.title: Generic
docs.text: The generic Linux distribution of Bifröst requires kernel support for PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, which is available since Linux 3.4. The effective minimum kernel can be higher for newer architectures. The binary does not require other shared libraries to be installed, regardless of whether the distribution is Ubuntu, Alpine, RedHat, or another variant. On the other hand, it lacks some features of the extended version.

docs.title: Extended
docs.text:
The extended Linux distribution of Bifröst currently only runs on Debian 12+, Ubuntu 22.04+ and Fedora 39+.

It does provide the following features:

  1. PAM authentication via Local authorization

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Name Shared-Lib Version GNU C Library (glibc) libc.so.6 2.34+ Linux PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules for Linux) libpam.so.0 1.4+

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
• Debian/Ubuntu: Usually installed by default, in some cases the following command might be necessary: 
    sudo apt install libpam0g -y
  • RedHat/Fedora: Already installed by default.

docs.title: Generic
docs.text: The generic macOS distribution of Bifröst contains all supported features for macOS 13 and later. It does not have any requirements on which other shared libraries need to be installed.

docs.title: Extended
docs.text: Not available.

docs.title: Generic
docs.text: The generic Windows distribution of Bifröst contains all supported features for Windows 10, Windows Server 2016, and later versions. It does not have any requirements on which other shared libraries need to be installed.

docs.title: Extended
docs.text: Not available.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: Bifröst can be either obtained as Archive which contains the binaries or as OCI/Docker images.

docs.title: Archives
docs.text:
Archives contain for every supported operating systems and architecture the binary of Bifröst itself with a basic README, licence information and demo material. It can be simply downloaded, extracted and run.

See the release page for all available downloads.
