docs.title: Compliance Artifacts
docs.text:
Every release provides platform- and edition-specific third-party notices and SBOMs alongside its archives. Archive SBOMs describe the downloadable archive; OCI SBOMs describe the indicated platform image within the multi-platform OCI index. They are intentionally separate because their package inventories and subject digests can differ.

The generic darwin/amd64 and darwin/arm64 release variants each include their architecture-specific archive, .third-party-notices.txt file, and archive .spdx.json and .cdx.json SBOMs. They have no OCI images or OCI SBOMs.

The release manifest relates every artifact to its platform, edition, media type and SHA-256 digest. Use the checksum file to verify all downloadable release assets.

The included license notices also cover the browser components.

Variant Notice Archive OCI Download SPDX CycloneDX Reference SPDX CycloneDX darwin/amd64/generic - - - darwin/arm64/generic - - - linux/386/extended - - - linux/386/generic linux/amd64/extended linux/amd64/generic linux/arm64/extended linux/arm64/generic linux/armv6/generic linux/armv7/extended linux/armv7/generic linux/riscv64/generic windows/amd64/generic windows/arm64/generic - - -

OCI entries link to the container package. The abbreviated digest identifies the immutable multi-platform index; the complete index and platform references are available in the release manifest.

docs.title: Installing in Docker
docs.text:
Tip

This guide shows how to install Bifröst in Docker/Container. If you like to use Bifröst directly on your Host, see its documentation here.

docs.title: Before we start
docs.text:
Be sure Bifröst is supporting your Docker host, by checking the following matrix:

Cells express support in format of <generic>/<extended>. See our documentation of distributions of Bifröst to learn more.

Architecture linux darwin windows i386 / / / amd64 / / / armv6 / / / armv7 / / / arm64 / / / riscv64 / / /

In the majority of the cases you might run Linux or Windows on AMD64, which is supported.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Note

This guide assumes you have a Linux distribution with systemd running. This reflects the majority of all actual distributions, such as Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, ...

  1. Ensure you have a working docker instance installed.

  2. Configure Bifröst. For example download the demo configuration and adjust it to your needs (see documentation of configuration for the documentation about it): 

    sudo mkdir -p /etc/engity/bifroest/
sudo curl -sSLf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/configurations/simple-inside-docker.yaml -o /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml
# Adjust it to your needs
sudo vi /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml

  3. Enable Bifröst to always run on your system, by downloading our example service configuration: 

    sudo curl -sSLf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/systemd/bifroest-in-docker.service -o /etc/systemd/system/bifroest.service
# Adjust it to your needs
sudo vi /etc/systemd/system/bifroest.service

    Note

    On a release-specific documentation page, set Environment=IMAGE=ghcr.io/engity-com/bifroest:1.0.0-beta3 in the service file to run that release. Its default :latest selects a moving stable release, not an alpha or beta release.

  4. Reload the systemd daemon: 

    sudo systemctl daemon-reload

  5. Enable and start Bifröst: 

    sudo systemctl enable bifroest.service
sudo systemctl start bifroest.service

  6. If you're using the original demo configuration, Bifröst will print a demo password to its log files while startup. You can receive it with the following command: 

    docker logs bifroest

  7. Now you can log in to Bifröst the first time: 

    ssh demo@localhost

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Ensure you have a working docker instance installed.

    Note

    This guide assumes you're running a Linux host of Docker on Docker for Windows (default).

    Bifröst also supports Windows Containers (Windows native). The image is based on Nano Server LTSC 2022, so Microsoft's host and container version compatibility rules apply. You also have to adjust the path below accordingly.

  2. Open a Powershell Terminal with Administrator privileges.

  3. Configure Bifröst. For example download the demo configuration and adjust it to your needs (see documentation of configuration for the documentation about it): 

    mkdir -Force 'C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest'
curl -sSLf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/configurations/simple-inside-docker-windows.yaml -o 'C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest\configuration.yaml'
# Adjust it to your needs
notepad 'C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest\configuration.yaml'

  4. Enable and start Bifröst: 

    docker run -d --restart unless-stopped --name bifroest -p 22:22 -v //var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest:/etc/engity/bifroest -v C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest:/var/lib/engity/bifroest ghcr.io/engity-com/bifroest:1.0.0-beta3 run --log.colorMode=always

  5. Now you can log in to Bifröst the first time: 

    ssh demo@localhost

docs.title: What's next?
docs.text:
• Configuration details
  • Install on Host

docs.title: Installing on host
docs.text:
Bifröst runs as a host service on port 22. Sign in with an existing local user; the same configuration works on all three platforms.

Port 22 must be free: stop the existing SSH server first, and keep another way to access the machine.

SSH may warn that the server key changed; verify the change before continuing.

Use the archive from the same release as this page. These examples use AMD64 for Linux and Windows, ARM64 for macOS, and assume a fresh installation; for other systems see distributions, for upgrades see the upgrade notes.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Use the Linux extended edition and an existing local user:

curl -fLsS -o bifroest-linux-amd64-extended.tgz 'https://github.com/engity-com/bifroest/releases/download/v1.0.0-beta3/bifroest-linux-amd64-extended.tgz'
sudo tar -xzf bifroest-linux-amd64-extended.tgz -C /usr/bin bifroest
sudo install -d -m 0750 /etc/engity/bifroest
sudo curl -fLsS -o /etc/engity/bifroest/configuration.yaml 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/configurations/on-host.yaml'
sudo curl -fLsS -o /etc/systemd/system/bifroest.service 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/systemd/bifroest.service'
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now bifroest.service

Log in with that user's SSH key or password:

ssh "$USER@localhost"

If login fails, check sudo journalctl -u bifroest.service. To revert, run sudo systemctl disable --now bifroest.service and restart the previous SSH server.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Use the Windows generic edition and an existing local user (not a domain account).

# Do the following commands in an elevated PowerShell window
$archive = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'bifroest-windows-amd64-generic.zip'
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://github.com/engity-com/bifroest/releases/download/v1.0.0-beta3/bifroest-windows-amd64-generic.zip' -OutFile $archive
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force 'C:\Program Files\Engity\Bifroest' | Out-Null
Expand-Archive -LiteralPath $archive -DestinationPath 'C:\Program Files\Engity\Bifroest'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force 'C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest' | Out-Null
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/configurations/on-host.yaml' -OutFile 'C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest\configuration.yaml'
& 'C:\Program Files\Engity\Bifroest\bifroest.exe' service install --configuration 'C:\ProgramData\Engity\Bifroest\configuration.yaml'

Log in with that user's SSH key or password:

ssh "$env:USERNAME@localhost"

If login fails, check Windows Event Viewer. To revert, stop Bifröst with & 'C:\Program Files\Engity\Bifroest\bifroest.exe' service remove and restart the previous SSH server.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Use the macOS generic edition and an existing local user:

curl -fLsS -o bifroest-darwin-arm64-generic.tgz 'https://github.com/engity-com/bifroest/releases/download/v1.0.0-beta3/bifroest-darwin-arm64-generic.tgz'
sudo install -d /usr/local/bin
sudo tar -xzf bifroest-darwin-arm64-generic.tgz -C /usr/local/bin bifroest
sudo install -d -o root -g wheel -m 0750 '/Library/Application Support/Engity/Bifroest'
sudo curl -fLsS -o '/Library/Application Support/Engity/Bifroest/configuration.yaml' 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/engity-com/bifroest/v1.0.0-beta3/contrib/configurations/on-host.yaml'
sudo chown root:wheel '/Library/Application Support/Engity/Bifroest/configuration.yaml'
sudo chmod 0640 '/Library/Application Support/Engity/Bifroest/configuration.yaml'
sudo /usr/local/bin/bifroest service install

Log in with that user's SSH key or password:

ssh "$USER@localhost"

If login fails, check the logs in /Library/Logs/Engity/Bifroest. To revert, run sudo /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/com.engity.bifroest service remove and re-enable Remote Login.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Adjust flows, local authorization and session environments for your access policy.
  • Configure Docker or Kubernetes only if you need those environments.

docs.title: Operating model and availability
docs.text:
• Who operates it? You run the host service or container, supply configuration and keys, and maintain the identity provider and workload dependencies. Management acts on that instance; it does not provide fleet-wide or tenant-scoped administration.
  • What survives a restart? With durable storage, sessions and saved-access registrations can survive. Preserve keys and complete evidence repositories too; use the checklist below.
  • What happens if an instance fails? Reconnect to the same Bifröst endpoint and sign in on a healthy instance to continue working with the workload data available there. Bifröst sessions are not shared between instances; reconnecting starts a new execution, not the previous shell.2
  • Is HA built in? Not built in, but you can provide HA access by running independent instances behind a TCP load balancer such as HAProxy or NGINX stream. Prefer sticky sessions and a redundant load-balancer endpoint.

docs.title: Choose a deployment
docs.text:
Deployment What to plan One supervised instance Durable storage, backups and a tested restart. Existing connections are interrupted. Independent instances behind a TCP load balancer Sticky sessions for normal operation; health checks route reconnecting clients to a healthy instance. Use separate repositories and audit signing identities, and make required workload data reachable from each instance. Replacement using an instance's existing state Coordinate exclusive repository and workload ownership. Test recovery on your actual storage and infrastructure.

Keep repositories instance-local. Each repository has one writer.1 When replacing an instance using its existing state, prevent the old writer from accessing that state or its workloads first. Local locks are not cross-host fencing; never delete a lock file to force a second writer to start.

docs.title: Routing and probes
docs.text:
• Prepare the shared endpoint. Configure SSH host keys trusted by your clients. For HTTPS, use TCP/TLS passthrough and provision certificates for the shared domain on every backend.
  • Prefer sticky sessions. Keep browser requests and SSH-initiated OIDC approvals on the same instance during normal operation. Configure TCP persistence through HAProxy stick tables or NGINX upstream hashing.
  • Monitor each instance. Use readiness checks to take unavailable backends out of rotation. /ready reports new-access readiness, /status process liveness; also test an actual login.

docs.title: Restart or recover one instance
docs.text:
In a load-balanced deployment, take only the affected instance out of rotation; healthy instances can keep accepting connections. Keep an independent administration path and define acceptable recovery time and data loss.

  1. Block new traffic to this instance and stop its writer. Let users finish or disconnect their connections. Allow the configured SSH and HTTP shutdown budgets. A failed readiness probe is not proof that the old process has stopped.
  2. Copy or restore complete state while stopped: configuration and referenced keys, sessions, journals and signing identities, Recording repositories and ACME storage. Protect backups as credentials; back up workload data separately and keep decryption private keys offline. Remote sealed artifacts alone are not a service backup.
  3. Check identities and revocations. Retain the matching host and signing keys. An older session backup can restore later-revoked saved access: reconcile it before reopening traffic. Perform upgrades separately from the first recovery attempt.
  4. Start one writer for the recovered state through its existing host service manager or container supervisor, initially with the same release and configuration. Inspect startup logs and check readiness directly; keep this instance out of rotation during acceptance checks. Resolve key or integrity errors instead of discarding repositories.
  5. Test before reopening:
    • Test workload access over each enabled transport: SSH, SSH over HTTPS and/or browser. Then test eligible saved access. Old browser access and pending logins must be rejected; a reusable session must reach the intended environment, not restore an old shell.
    • Verify retained evidence against independent producer trust and check remote delivery, if configured.
    • Test revocation and cleanup. Record recovery time and data gaps against your objectives, then return this instance to the pool.

Result: the recovered instance accepts new logins again. With healthy backends available, users can reconnect and continue working while the affected instance recovers; existing shells remain tied to their original instance.

  1. Process-lock and crash-reopen tests cover local filesystem ownership and recovery. ↩

  2. Instance-boundary tests and saved-access restart tests cover local-service isolation and resumption after restart. ↩

docs.title: Upgrade from v0.7.x to v1.0.0-beta3
docs.text: These notes apply to an upgrade from any v0.7.x release to v1.0.0-beta3. They document upgrade actions and behavior changes, not release notes. Patch releases within the new series share these upgrade notes.

docs.title: session.storage (filesystem)
docs.text:
The filesystem session repository now holds an exclusive operating-system lock. Before starting the upgraded Bifröst, stop every process using the same storage: only one process can open it at a time.

The lock file, .<storage-name>.bifroest.lock, is created next to the resolved storage directory. Check that its parent directory and any existing lock file are writable. Storage symlinks resolve to the same lock; a symlink pointing to a missing directory prevents startup. Existing session metadata needs no conversion.

docs.title: session.maxTimeout
docs.text:
If set, the maximum lifetime now counts from session creation rather than last access. Check active sessions and this setting before upgrading: some sessions may expire earlier or immediately.

Sessions saved by the previous minor series have no creation timestamp. For them, Bifröst uses the modification time of the session metadata file, which may differ from the actual creation time.

docs.title: flows[].name
docs.text: Flow names must be unique, may not be . or .., and may not exceed 255 bytes. Correct existing names that violate these rules before starting the upgraded version, or configuration validation will fail.

docs.title: RememberMe
docs.text: RememberMe now defaults to forbidden for local, simple, htpasswd and oidcDeviceAuth. Previously remembered SSH keys cannot resume access unless you enable it. Set rememberMe: allowedAndEnabledByDefault on the relevant authorization to retain automatic registration and reuse. Ordinary configured SSH keys remain valid. See RememberMe.

docs.title: OIDC Device Auth
docs.text:
OIDC now defaults to forceDisposeSessionOn: lostAccess and refreshToken.mode: proactive. Before upgrading, ensure your identity provider issues refresh tokens for the configured client and scopes (often requiring offline_access). Otherwise, new OIDC logins will be rejected. Bifröst does not add provider-specific scopes automatically.

Previously created sessions without a refresh token or recorded identity will be disposed when the upgraded service starts. Users of those sessions must authenticate again; running work may be interrupted.

To temporarily retain the previous behavior while configuring your identity provider, explicitly set both properties in the OIDC authorization:

forceDisposeSessionOn: never
refreshToken:
  mode: never

See the Device Authorization reference for the full configuration and examples.

docs.title: Execution environment variables
docs.text:
User-supplied variables now use the following precedence, with later sources overriding earlier ones:

  1. Variables accepted from the SSH client.
  2. Variables specified by an authorized_keys policy.
  3. Variables supplied by the authorization, including PAM.
  4. Variables configured for the environment.

Previously, SSH-client and authorized_keys variables could override authorization variables. Check policies that rely on colliding names. For Windows targets, names are case-insensitive: conflicting spellings in a single authorization or configured-environment map are rejected; repeated SSH-client names overwrite each other. Bifröst may set its own execution variables afterward.

docs.title: Existing IMP sessions
docs.text:
Containers and Pods from the previous minor series lack the required execution-lifecycle and IMP protocol revision metadata. A new login cannot reuse them and does not remove them. Housekeeping also checks active sessions: when it can establish incompatibility, it attempts to dispose the entire session, including the container or Pod and authorization. Running work may be interrupted.

You do not generally need to remove old resources yourself. Before starting the upgraded Bifröst, back up any needed container-local data, anonymous Docker volumes, and Pod-local ephemeral data. Persistent volumes have their own lifecycle. Invalid metadata, ambiguous ownership, and inspection or disposal failures require operator review. Changing resource metadata does not upgrade the IMP binary. See the Docker and Kubernetes details.

docs.title: Linux execution-scoped signals
docs.text: If you use execution-scoped signals in Linux containers or Pods, check for Linux 5.3 or newer and a seccomp profile allowing pidfd_open and pidfd_send_signal. Otherwise signal requests fail.

docs.title: Existing session cleanup tokens
docs.text:
Persisted local tokens from the previous minor series have no cleanup-token version field. Their account, home-directory, and process cleanup decisions are not migrated. Successful disposal can remove a token while leaving the account, home directory, and processes behind; the old identity snapshot is insufficient for safe deletion.

Before upgrading, identify accounts whose cleanup relied on existing sessions. Complete any needed cleanup before the upgrade, or afterward verify account identity, home ownership, and active sessions before reconciling them manually. Changing the new configuration cannot restore cleanup decisions in old tokens.

docs.title: environment.dispose.*
docs.text:
The previous minor series accepted these Linux local settings, which the upgraded version rejects if explicitly set:

  • dispose.deleteManagedUser: review deleteOnDispose.
  • dispose.deleteManagedUserHomeDir: review deleteHomeTogetherWithUser.
  • dispose.killManagedUserProcesses: review killProcessesOnDispose.

Remove the old settings before starting the upgraded version. Choose the top-level policies deliberately for new sessions: these are not one-to-one renames, since defaults and managed-user identification have changed. Account deletion now defaults to false.

docs.title: environment.killProcessesOnDispose
docs.text:
Process cleanup now defaults to {{ .user.managed }}. For newly managed accounts it can run even without account deletion and may terminate other processes owned by that account. Review this policy before upgrading; set killProcessesOnDispose: false if that is not intended.

When process cleanup applies, it requires pidfd_open and pidfd_send_signal (Linux 5.3 or newer, with both syscalls allowed by the security profile). If unavailable, cleanup fails closed and a dependent account deletion does not proceed. Disabling process cleanup avoids this prerequisite but may leave processes running.

docs.title: environment.name or environment.uid
docs.text:
Every Windows local flow must now select a local SAM account by name or SID. Without an account selection, shell and SFTP previously ran as the Bifröst service identity (often LocalSystem); the upgraded version rejects that configuration. By default the account must exist; creating one requires an explicit createIfAbsent policy.

For example, if a simple authorization entry names an existing local account:

environment:
  type: local
  name: "{{.authorization.entry.name}}"

For OIDC, map a verified claim to the account name; an email address is not automatically a Windows account name. With the account-management defaults in this example, Bifröst does not create, modify, or delete local users.

docs.title: Service identity and existing sessions
docs.text: Run Bifröst as LocalSystem for S4U session process startup, and check the selected account's permissions. S4U does not provide that account's network credentials or EFS access; check workloads that previously relied on the service identity. Saved Windows local sessions without a bound account SID cannot be reused and require reauthorization.
